0.title: Esther: The Hidden Hand
0.overview:
The book of Esther never names God. In the ESV of its ten chapters the words God, LORD, pray and heaven do not occur once. No prophet speaks, no miracle happens, and no one is said to pray. When the book was later translated into Greek, the translators added prayers and put the name of the Lord into the story; the Hebrew text, which our Bibles follow, leaves it out. And yet by the last chapter no reader can doubt who has been at work. Esther is the Bible's picture of how God is present in most of his people's lives: not in burning bushes, but in the timing of things.

It is set in Susa under Ahasuerus, the Persian king the Greeks called Xerxes (486-465 BC), a generation before Nehemiah served his son in the same palace. Its Jews are the ones who did not go home. An orphan, Hadassah, called Esther, is taken into the king's harem and made queen, keeping her people secret; her cousin Mordecai, a Benjaminite of the family of Kish, will not bow to Haman the Agagite; and Haman, by lot and by decree, sets a day eleven months away for every Jew in the empire to be killed. The old war between Israel and Amalek, left unfinished by Saul son of Kish when he spared Agag (1 Sam 15), is fought again in the Persian court.

Then everything turns. Mordecai puts on sackcloth; Esther, told that she may have come to the kingdom for such a time as this, goes to the king uncalled — if I perish, I perish (4:14, 16). A king cannot sleep, and the page of the royal chronicles read to him is the one about Mordecai. Haman is made to lead his enemy's horse through the city, and then is hanged on the gallows he built for him. A decree that cannot be revoked is answered by another. On the day chosen for the Jews' destruction the reverse occurred (9:1), and Haman's lots give their name to the feast of Purim. Mourning, fasting, weeping and lamenting are exchanged for light and gladness and joy and honour.

The book is honest about hard things, and this commentary tries to be too. Esther eats the king's food and conceals her people where Daniel refused; the narrator records it without comment, and God uses a young woman in a situation she did not choose. Chapter 9 records the Jews killing their enemies across the empire; the text frames it as defence against those who came to kill them, says three times that they took no plunder, and makes the feast the day they rested, not the day they fought. The church is given no such sword (2 Cor 10:4).

And the book is full of Christ, though it names no one but Persians and Jews. Esther going in uncalled to plead for a condemned people is a shadow of the Intercessor who went knowing he would die, and through whom we draw near to the throne of grace with confidence (Heb 4:16). Haman's tree, raised for the righteous man, held the guilty; at the cross the tree meant for the guilty held the Righteous One, who bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Pet 2:24). A sentence that could not be revoked was answered by another word: There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Rom 8:1). And the King who delights to honour his Son says of those who serve him, the Father will honor him (John 12:26).

The book ends with Mordecai second to the king, seeking the welfare of his people and speaking peace (10:3). God is not named in the last sentence either. His hand has been on every page.

1.title: The Banquet, the Queen, and the Empty Throne
1.text: <sup>1</sup>Now in the days of Ahasuerus, the Ahasuerus who reigned from India to Ethiopia over 127 provinces,<sup>2</sup>in those days when King Ahasuerus sat on his royal throne in Susa, the citadel,<sup>3</sup>in the third year of his reign he gave a feast for all his officials and servants. The army of Persia and Media and the nobles and governors of the provinces were before him,<sup>4</sup>while he showed the riches of his royal glory and the splendor and pomp of his greatness for many days, 180 days.<sup>5</sup>And when these days were completed, the king gave for all the people present in Susa the citadel, both great and small, a feast lasting for seven days in the court of the garden of the king's palace.<sup>6</sup>There were white cotton curtains and violet hangings fastened with cords of fine linen and purple to silver rods and marble pillars, and also couches of gold and silver on a mosaic pavement of porphyry, marble, mother-of-pearl, and precious stones.<sup>7</sup>Drinks were served in golden vessels, vessels of different kinds, and the royal wine was lavished according to the bounty of the king.<sup>8</sup>And drinking was according to this edict: "There is no compulsion." For the king had given orders to all the staff of his palace to do as each man desired.<sup>9</sup>Queen Vashti also gave a feast for the women in the palace that belonged to King Ahasuerus.<sup>10</sup>On the seventh day, when the heart of the king was merry with wine, he commanded Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha and Abagtha, Zethar and Carkas, the seven eunuchs who served in the presence of King Ahasuerus,<sup>11</sup>to bring Queen Vashti before the king with her royal crown, in order to show the peoples and the princes her beauty, for she was lovely to look at.<sup>12</sup>But Queen Vashti refused to come at the king's command delivered by the eunuchs. At this the king became enraged, and his anger burned within him.<sup>13</sup>Then the king said to the wise men who knew the times (for this was the king's procedure toward all who were versed in law and judgment,<sup>14</sup>the men next to him being Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, the seven princes of Persia and Media, who saw the king's face, and sat first in the kingdom):<sup>15</sup>"According to the law, what is to be done to Queen Vashti, because she has not performed the command of King Ahasuerus delivered by the eunuchs?"<sup>16</sup>Then Memucan said in the presence of the king and the officials, "Not only against the king has Queen Vashti done wrong, but also against all the officials and all the peoples who are in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus.<sup>17</sup>For the queen's behavior will be made known to all women, causing them to look at their husbands with contempt, since they will say, 'King Ahasuerus commanded Queen Vashti to be brought before him, and she did not come.'<sup>18</sup>This very day the noble women of Persia and Media who have heard of the queen's behavior will say the same to all the king's officials, and there will be contempt and wrath in plenty.<sup>19</sup>If it please the king, let a royal order go out from him, and let it be written among the laws of the Persians and the Medes so that it may not be repealed, that Vashti is never again to come before King Ahasuerus. And let the king give her royal position to another who is better than she.<sup>20</sup>So when the decree made by the king is proclaimed throughout all his kingdom, for it is vast, all women will give honor to their husbands, high and low alike."<sup>21</sup>This advice pleased the king and the princes, and the king did as Memucan proposed.<sup>22</sup>He sent letters to all the royal provinces, to every province in its own script and to every people in its own language, that every man be master in his own household and speak according to the language of his people.
1.overview: Ahasuerus (Xerxes I, 486-465 BC), ruler of 127 provinces from India to Ethiopia, displays the riches of his royal glory for 180 days in Susa, then feasts the whole city for seven days among gold couches and golden cups, while Queen Vashti feasts the women (vv. 1-9). On the seventh day, merry with wine, he sends for Vashti to show off her beauty to his guests. She refuses, and he is enraged (vv. 10-12). His seven counsellors turn the refusal into a threat to every husband in the empire; on Memucan's advice an unrepealable decree removes Vashti and gives her place to another who is better than she — Samuel's words to Saul (1 Sam 15:28) — and letters go to every province that every man be master in his own household (vv. 13-22). God is not mentioned; a throne has been emptied.
1.theology:
God is not named in this book at all, and he is never absent from it. He rules through a drunken king's vanity, a queen's refusal and a counsellor's panic, as surely as through a parted sea. The irrevocable law introduced here, and the Saul-and-Agag words it borrows, are the machinery the rest of the story will run on.

Two kings and two feasts: Ahasuerus summons his queen to display her beauty for his glory; Christ gives himself for his bride to present her in splendor, and invites us to the marriage supper of the Lamb (Eph 5:25-27; Rev 19:9).
1.examples:
In the ESV of Esther the words God, LORD, pray and heaven never appear.

A 180-day display of glory, three years before the fleet was lost at Salamis.

Even the drinking was by royal decree: There is no compulsion.

The king who ruled 127 provinces could not bring his wife across a courtyard.

A Persian lawyer used Samuel's words about Saul.

The empire's post carried a decree that husbands must be respected.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Riches of His Royal Glory
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ahasuerus who reigned from India to Ethiopia over 127 provinces holds court in Susa the citadel (vv. 1-2). In the third year of his reign he feasts his officials and army for 180 days, showing the riches of his royal glory and the splendor and pomp of his greatness (vv. 3-4), then gives all Susa a seven-day feast in the palace garden among gold couches and golden cups, where drinking was according to this edict: There is no compulsion (vv. 5-8). Queen Vashti gives a feast for the women (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: The book opens on the most powerful man in the world at the height of his glory, and never mentions God. The reader is being taught to look for the hand that the story does not name.

verseByVerse.quote: Now in the days of Ahasuerus, the Ahasuerus who reigned from India to Ethiopia over 127 provinces, in those days when King Ahasuerus sat on his royal throne in Susa, the citadel, in the third year of his reign he gave a feast for all his officials and servants. The army of Persia and Media and the nobles and governors of the provinces were before him, while he showed the riches of his royal glory and the splendor and pomp of his greatness for many days, 180 days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now in the days of Ahasuerus, the Ahasuerus who reigned from India to Ethiopia over 127 provinces. Ahasuerus is the Hebrew form of the name the Greeks wrote as Xerxes, the Persian king who reigned from 486 to 465 BC. His empire ran from the Indus to the upper Nile. In those days when King Ahasuerus sat on his royal throne in Susa, the citadel — the same palace where, a generation later, a Jew named Nehemiah would hand his son the wine (Neh 1:1).

Before we go further, notice what this book will not say. In the ESV of Esther the words God, LORD, pray and heaven do not occur once. No prophet speaks, no miracle happens, no one is said to pray. God is never once named. And yet by the last chapter no reader can doubt who has been at work. This is how God is present in most of our lives: not in burning bushes, but in the timing of things.

In the third year of his reign he gave a feast for all his officials and servants ... while he showed the riches of his royal glory and the splendor and pomp of his greatness for many days, 180 days. Half a year of showing off. The third year of Xerxes was 483 BC, and within three years his great invasion of Greece had ended with his fleet destroyed at Salamis. The glory on display was not as solid as it looked.

verseByVerse.quote: And when these days were completed, the king gave for all the people present in Susa the citadel, both great and small, a feast lasting for seven days in the court of the garden of the king's palace. There were white cotton curtains and violet hangings fastened with cords of fine linen and purple to silver rods and marble pillars, and also couches of gold and silver on a mosaic pavement of porphyry, marble, mother-of-pearl, and precious stones. Drinks were served in golden vessels, vessels of different kinds, and the royal wine was lavished according to the bounty of the king. And drinking was according to this edict: "There is no compulsion." For the king had given orders to all the staff of his palace to do as each man desired.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when these days were completed, the king gave for all the people present in Susa the citadel, both great and small, a feast lasting for seven days in the court of the garden of the king's palace. The narrator lingers on the furnishings as if walking us through the garden: white and violet hangings on silver rods, marble pillars, couches of gold and silver on a pavement of porphyry and mother-of-pearl, and drinks were served in golden vessels, vessels of different kinds. Everyone in the city, great and small, drinking from gold.

And drinking was according to this edict: There is no compulsion. For the king had given orders to all the staff of his palace to do as each man desired. Even the drinking was by royal decree. This is a book full of decrees, and full of the phrase as it pleased: what the king desires is done. And notice the irony. At this feast no one is compelled to drink. In a few verses one person will be compelled to come, and will not.

The word feast comes nineteen times in the ESV of this short book. Kings decide things at feasts in Esther, usually with wine in them, and the whole story will turn on two small feasts given by a queen. Keep an eye on the tables.

verseByVerse.quote: Queen Vashti also gave a feast for the women in the palace that belonged to King Ahasuerus.
verseByVerse.commentary: Queen Vashti also gave a feast for the women in the palace that belonged to King Ahasuerus. One verse, and a queen with a household and a feast of her own. Notice the phrase: the palace that belonged to King Ahasuerus. Everything in this world belongs to the king — the palace, the cups, the provinces — and, he assumes, the queen.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the seventh day, when the heart of the king was merry with wine, he sends seven eunuchs to bring Queen Vashti with her royal crown, in order to show the peoples and the princes her beauty (vv. 10-11). But Queen Vashti refused to come at the king's command delivered by the eunuchs. At this the king became enraged, and his anger burned within him (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: The man who ruled 127 provinces could not bring one woman across a courtyard. The book does not tell us why she refused; it tells us that an empty throne was the result.

verseByVerse.quote: On the seventh day, when the heart of the king was merry with wine, he commanded Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha and Abagtha, Zethar and Carkas, the seven eunuchs who served in the presence of King Ahasuerus, to bring Queen Vashti before the king with her royal crown, in order to show the peoples and the princes her beauty, for she was lovely to look at. But Queen Vashti refused to come at the king's command delivered by the eunuchs. At this the king became enraged, and his anger burned within him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the seventh day, when the heart of the king was merry with wine, he commanded ... the seven eunuchs who served in the presence of King Ahasuerus, to bring Queen Vashti before the king with her royal crown, in order to show the peoples and the princes her beauty, for she was lovely to look at.

A week of wine, a hall full of men, and the king sends for his wife to be looked at. She is to be displayed like the golden cups: one more possession, the finest one. Lovely to look at is exactly what will be said of Esther in the next chapter (2:7). In this court, that is what a woman is for.

But Queen Vashti refused to come at the king's command delivered by the eunuchs. At this the king became enraged, and his anger burned within him. The narrator does not tell us why. He neither praises Vashti nor blames her, and we should not fill the silence with our own story. But he has shown us the summons, and the reader can see it for what it is.

A reader may be living inside a marriage where what is asked of her is degrading. Scripture's call to wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord, sits directly beside the call to husbands: love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Eph 5:22, 25). A summons to be paraded before drunken men is the opposite of that love, and no one is bound to obey a command to shame or sin: We must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29).

And here is the contrast the whole Bible draws. This king called for his queen to show off her beauty for his own glory. There is another King who gave himself for his bride, so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle (Eph 5:27), and whose feast is the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev 19:9). At his first feast, when the wine ran out at a village wedding, he quietly made more and manifested his glory (John 2:11). One king uses his bride to display his glory. The other spends his glory to make his bride beautiful.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–22 — So That It May Not Be Repealed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king asks his wise men what the law requires (vv. 13-15). Memucan warns that every wife in the empire will now despise her husband (vv. 16-18), and proposes an unrepealable decree: let the king give her royal position to another who is better than she (vv. 19-20). Letters go to every province in every language, that every man be master in his own household (vv. 21-22).
verseByVerse.theology: The law of the Medes and Persians could not be repealed. That is a comedy here, where it deposes a queen, and it will be a terror in chapter 3, where it condemns a people.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king said to the wise men who knew the times (for this was the king's procedure toward all who were versed in law and judgment, the men next to him being Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, the seven princes of Persia and Media, who saw the king's face, and sat first in the kingdom): "According to the law, what is to be done to Queen Vashti, because she has not performed the command of King Ahasuerus delivered by the eunuchs?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the king said to the wise men who knew the times (for this was the king's procedure toward all who were versed in law and judgment. Seven named princes, who saw the king's face, and sat first in the kingdom — the kind of council of seven that sent Ezra to Jerusalem under the next king (Ezra 7:14). The ruler of the world, publicly refused, turns to his lawyers: According to the law, what is to be done to Queen Vashti?

There is comedy in it, and the narrator means us to hear it. The most powerful man on earth cannot manage his own household without a meeting of the cabinet.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Memucan said in the presence of the king and the officials, "Not only against the king has Queen Vashti done wrong, but also against all the officials and all the peoples who are in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus. For the queen's behavior will be made known to all women, causing them to look at their husbands with contempt, since they will say, 'King Ahasuerus commanded Queen Vashti to be brought before him, and she did not come.' This very day the noble women of Persia and Media who have heard of the queen's behavior will say the same to all the king's officials, and there will be contempt and wrath in plenty. If it please the king, let a royal order go out from him, and let it be written among the laws of the Persians and the Medes so that it may not be repealed, that Vashti is never again to come before King Ahasuerus. And let the king give her royal position to another who is better than she. So when the decree made by the king is proclaimed throughout all his kingdom, for it is vast, all women will give honor to their husbands, high and low alike."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not only against the king has Queen Vashti done wrong, but also against all the officials and all the peoples who are in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus. For the queen's behavior will be made known to all women, causing them to look at their husbands with contempt. Memucan turns one refusal into a threat to every husband in the empire. This very day, he says, the noblewomen will be saying it at dinner.

If it please the king, let a royal order go out from him, and let it be written among the laws of the Persians and the Medes so that it may not be repealed. Here, for the first time, is the rule the whole plot will hang on. The law of the Medes and Persians could not be changed even by the king who made it (Dan 6:8, 15). Today it is used to depose a queen. In chapter 3 it will be used to sentence a nation to death, and even the king will not be able to take it back (8:8).

And let the king give her royal position to another who is better than she. Listen to that sentence with the rest of the Bible in your ear. When Saul spared Agag king of the Amalekites, Samuel told him, The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you this day and has given it to a neighbor of yours, who is better than you (1 Sam 15:28). The same words, from a Persian lawyer who had never heard of Samuel. And the Saul and Agag story is about to be played again: Mordecai will be introduced as a Benjaminite, son of Kish (2:5), Saul's own family, and his enemy as Haman the Agagite (3:1). The narrator never says God is arranging things. He lets the words say it.

verseByVerse.quote: This advice pleased the king and the princes, and the king did as Memucan proposed. He sent letters to all the royal provinces, to every province in its own script and to every people in its own language, that every man be master in his own household and speak according to the language of his people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This advice pleased the king and the princes, and the king did as Memucan proposed. He sent letters to all the royal provinces, to every province in its own script and to every people in its own language, that every man be master in his own household and speak according to the language of his people.

The whole imperial post, in every script from India to Ethiopia, is set moving to announce that husbands are in charge. It is the most powerful state on earth making itself ridiculous. A law can depose a queen; it cannot make anyone honour anyone. Respect cannot be decreed, and love less still.

Remember those couriers and those letters in every language. The same postal system will carry a decree of death to every province in chapter 3, and a decree of life in chapter 8. And the throne beside the king is now empty. The narrator does not say who will fill it or why. Nobody in Susa that night was thinking about the Jews. Someone was.

2.title: The Girl From Exile: Esther Comes to the Throne
2.text: <sup>1</sup>After these things, when the anger of King Ahasuerus had abated, he remembered Vashti and what she had done and what had been decreed against her.<sup>2</sup>Then the king's young men who attended him said, "Let beautiful young virgins be sought out for the king.<sup>3</sup>And let the king appoint officers in all the provinces of his kingdom to gather all the beautiful young virgins to the harem in Susa the citadel, under custody of Hegai, the king's eunuch, who is in charge of the women. Let their cosmetics be given them.<sup>4</sup>And let the young woman who pleases the king be queen instead of Vashti." This pleased the king, and he did so.<sup>5</sup>Now there was a Jew in Susa the citadel whose name was Mordecai, the son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, a Benjaminite,<sup>6</sup>who had been carried away from Jerusalem among the captives carried away with Jeconiah king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had carried away.<sup>7</sup>He was bringing up Hadassah, that is Esther, the daughter of his uncle, for she had neither father nor mother. The young woman had a beautiful figure and was lovely to look at, and when her father and her mother died, Mordecai took her as his own daughter.<sup>8</sup>So when the king's order and his edict were proclaimed, and when many young women were gathered in Susa the citadel in custody of Hegai, Esther also was taken into the king's palace and put in custody of Hegai, who had charge of the women.<sup>9</sup>And the young woman pleased him and won his favor. And he quickly provided her with her cosmetics and her portion of food, and with seven chosen young women from the king's palace, and advanced her and her young women to the best place in the harem.<sup>10</sup>Esther had not made known her people or kindred, for Mordecai had commanded her not to make it known.<sup>11</sup>And every day Mordecai walked in front of the court of the harem to learn how Esther was and what was happening to her.<sup>12</sup>Now when the turn came for each young woman to go in to King Ahasuerus, after being twelve months under the regulations for the women, since this was the regular period of their beautifying, six months with oil of myrrh and six months with spices and ointments for women—<sup>13</sup>when the young woman went in to the king in this way, she was given whatever she desired to take with her from the harem to the king's palace.<sup>14</sup>In the evening she would go in, and in the morning she would return to the second harem in custody of Shaashgaz, the king's eunuch, who was in charge of the concubines. She would not go in to the king again, unless the king delighted in her and she was summoned by name.<sup>15</sup>When the turn came for Esther the daughter of Abihail the uncle of Mordecai, who had taken her as his own daughter, to go in to the king, she asked for nothing except what Hegai the king's eunuch, who had charge of the women, advised. Now Esther was winning favor in the eyes of all who saw her.<sup>16</sup>And when Esther was taken to King Ahasuerus, into his royal palace, in the tenth month, which is the month of Tebeth, in the seventh year of his reign,<sup>17</sup>the king loved Esther more than all the women, and she won grace and favor in his sight more than all the virgins, so that he set the royal crown on her head and made her queen instead of Vashti.<sup>18</sup>Then the king gave a great feast for all his officials and servants; it was Esther's feast. He also granted a remission of taxes to the provinces and gave gifts with royal generosity.<sup>19</sup>Now when the virgins were gathered together the second time, Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate.<sup>20</sup>Esther had not made known her kindred or her people, as Mordecai had commanded her, for Esther obeyed Mordecai just as when she was brought up by him.<sup>21</sup>In those days, as Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate, Bigthan and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs, who guarded the threshold, became angry and sought to lay hands on King Ahasuerus.<sup>22</sup>And this came to the knowledge of Mordecai, and he told it to Queen Esther, and Esther told the king in the name of Mordecai.<sup>23</sup>When the affair was investigated and found to be so, the men were both hanged on the gallows. And it was recorded in the book of the chronicles in the presence of the king.
2.overview: With Vashti deposed, beautiful young women are gathered from every province into the king's harem, and whoever pleases him will be queen (vv. 1-4). Mordecai, a Benjaminite whose family names are Saul's, has raised his orphaned cousin Hadassah, Esther, as his own daughter (vv. 5-7). She is taken to the harem, wins the favour of Hegai, and on Mordecai's orders keeps her Jewish identity secret while he watches over her from outside (vv. 8-11). After a year of preparation each girl spends one night with the king and passes to the concubines' house for life unless called by name (vv. 12-14). Esther asks for nothing but what Hegai advises; in Xerxes' seventh year the king loves her above all and crowns her queen (vv. 15-18). Mordecai, at the king's gate, uncovers a plot against the king's life and reports it through Esther; the plotters are hanged, and the deed is recorded in the royal chronicles, unrewarded (vv. 19-23).
2.theology:
God is still unnamed, and his hand is everywhere: an orphan placed in the palace, favour given in the very words Genesis uses of the LORD's kindness to Joseph (Gen 39:21), a good deed filed in an archive to be found at the right moment. He works through people in situations they did not choose and do not always handle well, without approving everything they do.

Mordecai takes an orphan as his own daughter; God adopts orphans as sons through his Son (Gal 4:5; John 14:18). And nothing done for him is lost: a book of remembrance was written before him (Mal 3:16).
2.examples:
Mordecai's family names are the names of Saul's family.

The exile with Jeconiah was 118 years before Esther became queen.

Hadassah means myrtle.

Every day Mordecai walked past the harem wall to ask how she was.

For the girls not chosen: the second harem for life.

Esther took only what she was advised to take.

The favour she won is described in the words used of the LORD's kindness to Joseph.

Mordecai saved the king's life and got a line in the annals.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Let the Young Woman Who Pleases the King Be Queen
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When his anger has cooled, the king remembered Vashti and what she had done and what had been decreed against her (v. 1). His young men propose that beautiful young virgins be gathered from every province into the harem at Susa, and let the young woman who pleases the king be queen instead of Vashti. This pleased the king, and he did so (vv. 2-4).
verseByVerse.theology: The empire that could not repeal a law begins to replace a queen, by gathering young women from 127 provinces like tribute. The story is about to put a Jewish orphan in the middle of it.

verseByVerse.quote: After these things, when the anger of King Ahasuerus had abated, he remembered Vashti and what she had done and what had been decreed against her. Then the king's young men who attended him said, "Let beautiful young virgins be sought out for the king. And let the king appoint officers in all the provinces of his kingdom to gather all the beautiful young virgins to the harem in Susa the citadel, under custody of Hegai, the king's eunuch, who is in charge of the women. Let their cosmetics be given them. And let the young woman who pleases the king be queen instead of Vashti." This pleased the king, and he did so.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After these things, when the anger of King Ahasuerus had abated, he remembered Vashti and what she had done and what had been decreed against her. The wine has worn off and the anger with it. He remembers her. But the decree cannot be repealed. The law that was supposed to show the king's power has trapped him.

His young men have a remedy: Let beautiful young virgins be sought out for the king. Officers in every province are to gather them to the harem in Susa, and let the young woman who pleases the king be queen instead of Vashti. This pleased the king, and he did so.

Call it what it is. Girls taken from their families in every province of the empire, brought to the palace as a king's selection. The narrator does not stop to condemn it, but he does not dress it up either. And into the middle of this he is about to set a Jewish orphan.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Mordecai, a Benjaminite son of Kish, of a family deported with Jeconiah, has brought up his orphaned cousin Hadassah, that is Esther, as his own daughter (vv. 5-7). She is taken into the harem, where Hegai favours her; on Mordecai's orders she does not reveal her people, and he walks past the harem court every day to hear how she is (vv. 8-11). After twelve months of preparation each young woman has one night with the king (vv. 12-14). Esther asks for nothing but what Hegai advises, and the king loved Esther more than all the women, set the royal crown on her head and made her queen, with a great feast (vv. 15-18).
verseByVerse.theology: The words for favor and grace in this chapter are the two words Genesis uses when the LORD was with Joseph and showed him steadfast love and gave him favor (Gen 39:21). Esther uses them and never says who gave them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a Jew in Susa the citadel whose name was Mordecai, the son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, a Benjaminite, who had been carried away from Jerusalem among the captives carried away with Jeconiah king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had carried away. He was bringing up Hadassah, that is Esther, the daughter of his uncle, for she had neither father nor mother. The young woman had a beautiful figure and was lovely to look at, and when her father and her mother died, Mordecai took her as his own daughter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now there was a Jew in Susa the citadel whose name was Mordecai, the son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, a Benjaminite. Every Israelite reader would hear those names. There was a man of Benjamin whose name was Kish: that is how the story of Saul begins (1 Sam 9:1). Shimei was the name of the man of Saul's house who cursed David on his flight from Absalom (2 Sam 16:5). Mordecai comes from the family of Israel's first king. Keep that in mind until the next chapter introduces his enemy.

Who had been carried away from Jerusalem among the captives carried away with Jeconiah king of Judah. Jeconiah went into exile in 597 BC (2 Kgs 24:12). Esther is taken to the king in 479 BC (v. 16). That is 118 years, so the one who was carried away must be the family's ancestor, most naturally Kish, and not Mordecai himself. Mordecai is the great-grandson of the exile, born in Persia, a Jew who never went home.

He was bringing up Hadassah, that is Esther, the daughter of his uncle, for she had neither father nor mother ... and when her father and her mother died, Mordecai took her as his own daughter. She has two names. Hadassah is Hebrew for myrtle, the tree Isaiah promised would grow instead of the brier (Isa 55:13); Esther is her Persian name, perhaps meaning star. A Jewish girl with a Persian name, an orphan taken in by her cousin and brought up as his daughter.

Many readers know what it is to lose a father or mother, or to have been raised by someone who did not have to take them in. Mordecai's kindness is a small picture of a larger one: God sent his Son to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons (Gal 4:5), and the Son promised, I will not leave you as orphans (John 14:18).

verseByVerse.quote: So when the king's order and his edict were proclaimed, and when many young women were gathered in Susa the citadel in custody of Hegai, Esther also was taken into the king's palace and put in custody of Hegai, who had charge of the women. And the young woman pleased him and won his favor. And he quickly provided her with her cosmetics and her portion of food, and with seven chosen young women from the king's palace, and advanced her and her young women to the best place in the harem. Esther had not made known her people or kindred, for Mordecai had commanded her not to make it known. And every day Mordecai walked in front of the court of the harem to learn how Esther was and what was happening to her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So when the king's order and his edict were proclaimed ... Esther also was taken into the king's palace and put in custody of Hegai. Was taken. The verb is passive. She did not enter a contest; she was collected.

And the young woman pleased him and won his favor. And he quickly provided her with her cosmetics and her portion of food. The word for favor here is hesed, the Old Testament's great word for God's steadfast love. A eunuch in a pagan harem shows it to a Jewish girl, and the text does not say why.

Here is a hard question, and it should be faced honestly. Esther eats the king's food. Daniel, taken to a pagan court a century earlier, resolved that he would not defile himself with the king's food (Dan 1:8). She keeps her people secret, and in time she will spend a night with a pagan king. The narrator makes no comment at all. Esther is not presented as a model of Daniel's kind of resistance. She is a young woman in a situation she did not choose, doing what the people around her advise. And God does not wait for his people to handle everything well before he uses them. That is not permission to compromise. It is mercy for those who already have.

Esther had not made known her people or kindred, for Mordecai had commanded her not to make it known. And every day Mordecai walked in front of the court of the harem to learn how Esther was and what was happening to her. Why Mordecai insisted on silence, we are not told; the next chapter will show what one man in power could do to a people he hated. He could not get her out. So every day he walked past the wall that held her, asking for news. It is a picture of helpless love that will not stop caring.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the turn came for each young woman to go in to King Ahasuerus, after being twelve months under the regulations for the women, since this was the regular period of their beautifying, six months with oil of myrrh and six months with spices and ointments for women— when the young woman went in to the king in this way, she was given whatever she desired to take with her from the harem to the king's palace. In the evening she would go in, and in the morning she would return to the second harem in custody of Shaashgaz, the king's eunuch, who was in charge of the concubines. She would not go in to the king again, unless the king delighted in her and she was summoned by name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when the turn came for each young woman to go in to King Ahasuerus, after being twelve months under the regulations for the women, since this was the regular period of their beautifying, six months with oil of myrrh and six months with spices and ointments. A year of preparation for one night.

In the evening she would go in, and in the morning she would return to the second harem in custody of Shaashgaz, the king's eunuch, who was in charge of the concubines. She would not go in to the king again, unless the king delighted in her and she was summoned by name. For every girl not chosen, that was her life: the second harem, a concubine for ever, never to marry, never to go home, waiting to be called by name and almost certainly never called. The narrator states it in one flat sentence. The cruelty is in the flatness.

verseByVerse.quote: When the turn came for Esther the daughter of Abihail the uncle of Mordecai, who had taken her as his own daughter, to go in to the king, she asked for nothing except what Hegai the king's eunuch, who had charge of the women, advised. Now Esther was winning favor in the eyes of all who saw her. And when Esther was taken to King Ahasuerus, into his royal palace, in the tenth month, which is the month of Tebeth, in the seventh year of his reign, the king loved Esther more than all the women, and she won grace and favor in his sight more than all the virgins, so that he set the royal crown on her head and made her queen instead of Vashti. Then the king gave a great feast for all his officials and servants; it was Esther's feast. He also granted a remission of taxes to the provinces and gave gifts with royal generosity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the turn came for Esther ... to go in to the king, she asked for nothing except what Hegai the king's eunuch, who had charge of the women, advised. Now Esther was winning favor in the eyes of all who saw her. At the moment she goes in, the narrator gives the orphan's father a name: Esther the daughter of Abihail. She is somebody's daughter. Every other girl could take whatever she desired (v. 13). Esther took only what she was advised to take. She did not grasp.

In the tenth month, which is the month of Tebeth, in the seventh year of his reign. The feast of chapter 1 was in the third year. Four years have passed: the years in which Xerxes led his armies into Greece and came home defeated. The king who sat down with Esther had lost a war.

The king loved Esther more than all the women, and she won grace and favor in his sight more than all the virgins, so that he set the royal crown on her head and made her queen instead of Vashti. Grace and favor are, in Hebrew, chen and hesed: the two words Genesis uses of Joseph in prison, the LORD was with Joseph and showed him steadfast love and gave him favor (Gen 39:21). In Genesis the giver is named. In Esther he is not, and the words are the same. That is how this whole book talks about God.

Then the king gave a great feast ... it was Esther's feast. He also granted a remission of taxes to the provinces. An orphan of the exile, with no family but a cousin at the gate, wears the crown of Persia. She was a queen now, and nobody in the palace knew she was a Jew.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–23 — Recorded in the Book of the Chronicles
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Mordecai sits at the king's gate, and Esther still keeps her people secret (vv. 19-20). Two of the king's eunuchs plot to kill him; Mordecai learns of it and tells Esther, who tells the king in Mordecai's name. The men are hanged, and it was recorded in the book of the chronicles in the presence of the king (vv. 21-23).
verseByVerse.theology: A life saved, and no reward given. The deed goes into a book and is forgotten by everyone but the One the book never names. It will be read aloud on the right night (6:1-3).

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the virgins were gathered together the second time, Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate. Esther had not made known her kindred or her people, as Mordecai had commanded her, for Esther obeyed Mordecai just as when she was brought up by him.
verseByVerse.commentary: Now when the virgins were gathered together the second time, Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate. A second gathering of girls, after Esther had been crowned. The harem went on filling; the king's appetite had not changed. Esther's crown did not make her secure, and in chapter 4 she will say she has not been called to the king for thirty days (4:11). The gate was where officials sat and business was done; Mordecai had some post in the king's service. Esther had not made known her kindred or her people, as Mordecai had commanded her, for Esther obeyed Mordecai just as when she was brought up by him. Queen of Persia, and still doing what her cousin told her. That habit of trust between them is what the whole deliverance will run on.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days, as Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate, Bigthan and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs, who guarded the threshold, became angry and sought to lay hands on King Ahasuerus. And this came to the knowledge of Mordecai, and he told it to Queen Esther, and Esther told the king in the name of Mordecai. When the affair was investigated and found to be so, the men were both hanged on the gallows. And it was recorded in the book of the chronicles in the presence of the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In those days, as Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate, Bigthan and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs, who guarded the threshold, became angry and sought to lay hands on King Ahasuerus. Two of the men who guarded the door of the king's rooms plotted to murder him. Mordecai heard of it and told Esther, and Esther told the king in the name of Mordecai.

When the affair was investigated and found to be so, the men were both hanged on the gallows. And it was recorded in the book of the chronicles in the presence of the king. The word for gallows is simply wood, a tree; it will appear again, fifty cubits high, in chapter 5. And the last words of the chapter are about a book. Mordecai saved the king's life, and nothing happened to him. No reward, no promotion, not even thanks. A clerk wrote a line in the annals, and everybody forgot.

Anyone who has done a costly good thing and seen it vanish without a word of thanks knows this sentence. The book of Esther is about to show that in God's world nothing recorded is lost. Malachi says the same of those who fear the LORD: a book of remembrance was written before him (Mal 3:16). The Persian clerk thought he was filing a routine report. He was placing the most important page of the story exactly where a sleepless king would one day find it (6:1-2).

3.title: The Decree of Death: Haman's Plot Against the Jews
3.text: <sup>1</sup>After these things King Ahasuerus promoted Haman the Agagite, the son of Hammedatha, and advanced him and set his throne above all the officials who were with him.<sup>2</sup>And all the king's servants who were at the king's gate bowed down and paid homage to Haman, for the king had so commanded concerning him. But Mordecai did not bow down or pay homage.<sup>3</sup>Then the king's servants who were at the king's gate said to Mordecai, "Why do you transgress the king's command?"<sup>4</sup>And when they spoke to him day after day and he would not listen to them, they told Haman, in order to see whether Mordecai's words would stand, for he had told them that he was a Jew.<sup>5</sup>And when Haman saw that Mordecai did not bow down or pay homage to him, Haman was filled with fury.<sup>6</sup>But he disdained to lay hands on Mordecai alone. So, as they had made known to him the people of Mordecai, Haman sought to destroy all the Jews, the people of Mordecai, throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus.<sup>7</sup>In the first month, which is the month of Nisan, in the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus, they cast Pur (that is, they cast lots) before Haman day after day; and they cast it month after month till the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar.<sup>8</sup>Then Haman said to King Ahasuerus, "There is a certain people scattered abroad and dispersed among the peoples in all the provinces of your kingdom. Their laws are different from those of every other people, and they do not keep the king's laws, so that it is not to the king's profit to tolerate them.<sup>9</sup>If it please the king, let it be decreed that they be destroyed, and I will pay 10,000 talents of silver into the hands of those who have charge of the king's business, that they may put it into the king's treasuries."<sup>10</sup>So the king took his signet ring from his hand and gave it to Haman the Agagite, the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews.<sup>11</sup>And the king said to Haman, "The money is given to you, the people also, to do with them as it seems good to you."<sup>12</sup>Then the king's scribes were summoned on the thirteenth day of the first month, and an edict, according to all that Haman commanded, was written to the king's satraps and to the governors over all the provinces and to the officials of all the peoples, to every province in its own script and every people in its own language. It was written in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed with the king's signet ring.<sup>13</sup>Letters were sent by couriers to all the king's provinces with instruction to destroy, to kill, and to annihilate all Jews, young and old, women and children, in one day, the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar, and to plunder their goods.<sup>14</sup>A copy of the document was to be issued as a decree in every province by proclamation to all the peoples to be ready for that day.<sup>15</sup>The couriers went out hurriedly by order of the king, and the decree was issued in Susa the citadel. And the king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was thrown into confusion.
3.overview: The king promotes Haman the Agagite above all his officials, and everyone bows to him — except Mordecai, a Jew of the family of Kish, who will not bow to a descendant of Agag (vv. 1-4). Haman, enraged, decides to destroy not Mordecai alone but every Jew in the empire (vv. 5-6). In Nisan, the month of Passover, lots (Pur) are cast to choose the day, and the lot falls eleven months later, in Adar (v. 7). Haman tells the king of an unnamed people with different laws who do not keep the king's, and offers 10,000 talents of silver; the king hands him the signet ring and the people (vv. 8-11). On the eve of Passover the decree is written in every language to destroy, kill and annihilate all Jews, young and old, women and children, on one day, and plunder their goods (vv. 12-14). The king and Haman sit down to drink while Susa is thrown into confusion (v. 15).
3.theology:
The ancient war with Amalek, left unfinished by Saul (1 Sam 15), returns: an Agagite turns the sentence once given against Amalek on the people of God. Behind it is the enmity of Gen 3:15, the attempt to destroy the people from whom the Messiah would come.

Haman cast lots for the day of death; its every decision is from the LORD (Prov 16:33). The decree written on the eve of Passover would be undone, and its lots would name the feast of deliverance. The powerful who drank over a death sentence prefigure the rulers who became friends over the condemnation of Christ (Luke 23:12).
3.examples:
The man who saved the king got nothing; Haman was promoted for nothing.

The son of Kish would not bow to the Agagite.

Haman never named the people he wanted destroyed.

The lot was cast in the month of Passover; the decree was written on its eve.

Ten thousand talents: about three hundred tons of silver.

The king gave away a people without asking who they were — his own queen among them.

The king and Haman sat down to drink; the city was thrown into confusion.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Mordecai Did Not Bow Down
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king promotes Haman the Agagite above all his officials, and everyone at the king's gate bows to him by royal command. But Mordecai did not bow down or pay homage (vv. 1-2). Asked day after day why he disobeys, he tells them he is a Jew, and they report him (vv. 3-4). Haman was filled with fury. But he disdained to lay hands on Mordecai alone, and sets out to destroy all the Jews throughout the kingdom (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: The son of Kish will not bow to the Agagite. An old war, begun in the wilderness and left unfinished by Saul, has come back to life in the Persian court.

verseByVerse.quote: After these things King Ahasuerus promoted Haman the Agagite, the son of Hammedatha, and advanced him and set his throne above all the officials who were with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After these things King Ahasuerus promoted Haman the Agagite, the son of Hammedatha, and advanced him and set his throne above all the officials who were with him.

After these things: after Mordecai saved the king's life and received nothing (2:23). The man who deserved honour is left at the gate; a man of whom we are told nothing is raised above everyone. That is how the world often looks. The book is not going to leave it there.

The Agagite. For a Jewish reader, that one word is enough. Agag was the king of the Amalekites, the people who fell on Israel's stragglers in the wilderness, when you were faint and weary (Deut 25:18), and of whom God said, The LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation (Exod 17:16). Saul, son of Kish, was sent to finish that war, and spared Agag (1 Sam 15:9). Now Mordecai, son of Kish, meets Haman, almost certainly of the line of Agag. More than five hundred years later, in Persia, the war Saul left unfinished is about to be fought again.

verseByVerse.quote: And all the king's servants who were at the king's gate bowed down and paid homage to Haman, for the king had so commanded concerning him. But Mordecai did not bow down or pay homage. Then the king's servants who were at the king's gate said to Mordecai, "Why do you transgress the king's command?" And when they spoke to him day after day and he would not listen to them, they told Haman, in order to see whether Mordecai's words would stand, for he had told them that he was a Jew.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And all the king's servants who were at the king's gate bowed down and paid homage to Haman, for the king had so commanded concerning him. But Mordecai did not bow down or pay homage.

Why not? Israelites bowed to kings and great men without sin: David bowed to Saul with his face to the ground (1 Sam 24:8), and Abraham bowed to the Hittites (Gen 23:7). So the bow itself was not the problem. The only reason the text gives is in verse 4: he had told them that he was a Jew. A Jew, son of Kish, would not bow to an Agagite. Whether there was more to it, divine honours claimed by Haman or simply the old enmity, the narrator does not say, and he does not say that Mordecai was wrong.

Then the king's servants who were at the king's gate said to Mordecai, Why do you transgress the king's command? And when they spoke to him day after day and he would not listen to them, they told Haman, in order to see whether Mordecai's words would stand. Day after day, the pressure of colleagues: everybody else does it; why won't you? Most of us know that kind of pressure at work. Mordecai stood in it quietly, and it cost him far more than he could have guessed.

That is the hard part of this chapter for a believer. Faithfulness does not always make things safer, and sometimes it puts others at risk too. Mordecai's refusal would bring a death sentence on every Jew in the empire. Jesus told his disciples to expect such things: If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you (John 15:18).

verseByVerse.quote: And when Haman saw that Mordecai did not bow down or pay homage to him, Haman was filled with fury. But he disdained to lay hands on Mordecai alone. So, as they had made known to him the people of Mordecai, Haman sought to destroy all the Jews, the people of Mordecai, throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when Haman saw that Mordecai did not bow down or pay homage to him, Haman was filled with fury. But he disdained to lay hands on Mordecai alone. So, as they had made known to him the people of Mordecai, Haman sought to destroy all the Jews, the people of Mordecai, throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus.

One man would not bow, and a whole people is sentenced. Killing Mordecai alone was beneath Haman's dignity; a grievance that size needed a nation to satisfy it. That is the logic of every genocide in history: a personal hatred given the power of a state. And behind this particular hatred the Bible sees the oldest war of all, the enmity between the serpent and the offspring of the woman (Gen 3:15). To destroy all the Jews would have been to destroy the family from which the Messiah was to come.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–15 — To Destroy, to Kill, and to Annihilate
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In Nisan of the twelfth year the lot, Pur, is cast before Haman and falls on Adar (v. 7). He tells the king of a certain people scattered abroad who keep their own laws, and offers 10,000 talents of silver for their destruction (vv. 8-9). The king gives him his signet ring: The money is given to you, the people also (vv. 10-11). On the thirteenth of Nisan the decree goes out in every script and language, to destroy, to kill, and to annihilate all Jews, young and old, women and children, in one day (vv. 12-14). And the king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was thrown into confusion (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: The lot was cast in the month of Passover and the decree was written on its eve. The Jews of the empire would hear their death sentence as they prepared to remember their deliverance from Egypt.

verseByVerse.quote: In the first month, which is the month of Nisan, in the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus, they cast Pur (that is, they cast lots) before Haman day after day; and they cast it month after month till the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the first month, which is the month of Nisan, in the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus, they cast Pur (that is, they cast lots) before Haman day after day; and they cast it month after month till the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar.

The twelfth year is five years after Esther was crowned (2:16). And the month is Nisan, the month of Passover, when every Jewish household remembered the night God struck Egypt and brought his people out. In that month an Agagite sat with his diviners casting lots to find the right day to wipe them out.

Pur is a Babylonian word for a lot, explained for the reader in the verse itself, and it will give the festival its name: Purim, Lots (9:24-26). Haman consulted chance to choose the day of death. The lot fell on Adar, eleven months away, time for everything that follows. Haman trusted the dice. Proverbs had already said who throws them: The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD (Prov 16:33).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Haman said to King Ahasuerus, "There is a certain people scattered abroad and dispersed among the peoples in all the provinces of your kingdom. Their laws are different from those of every other people, and they do not keep the king's laws, so that it is not to the king's profit to tolerate them. If it please the king, let it be decreed that they be destroyed, and I will pay 10,000 talents of silver into the hands of those who have charge of the king's business, that they may put it into the king's treasuries."
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is a certain people scattered abroad and dispersed among the peoples in all the provinces of your kingdom. Their laws are different from those of every other people, and they do not keep the king's laws, so that it is not to the king's profit to tolerate them.

Listen to how it is done. He never names them. A certain people. He mixes truth with lies: their laws were different; they kept a Sabbath and ate differently and worshipped one God. But they do not keep the king's laws was false, except for one man at one gate refusing one bow. And he closes with the argument that moves kings: it does not pay to tolerate them.

Christians should recognise the charge. The church too is a certain people scattered abroad; Peter writes to believers as elect exiles of the Dispersion (1 Pet 1:1). Its laws are different, and it has often been accused of not keeping the king's.

If it please the king, let it be decreed that they be destroyed, and I will pay 10,000 talents of silver. A talent weighed some thirty kilograms or more; ten thousand of them is about three hundred tons of silver. Haman was ready to pay a fortune out of his own estate to see his grudge satisfied.

verseByVerse.quote: So the king took his signet ring from his hand and gave it to Haman the Agagite, the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews. And the king said to Haman, "The money is given to you, the people also, to do with them as it seems good to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the king took his signet ring from his hand and gave it to Haman the Agagite, the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews. The ring made a document the king's own. With it went the power of life and death over millions. And the narrator gives Haman his title for the first time: the enemy of the Jews.

And the king said to Haman, The money is given to you, the people also, to do with them as it seems good to you. The king does not ask who this people is. He does not ask what they have done. He does not want the silver. He simply hands a nation to the man who hates them. It is not even cruelty; it is indifference, which has killed as many as cruelty ever has. And his own queen was one of the people he had just given away.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king's scribes were summoned on the thirteenth day of the first month, and an edict, according to all that Haman commanded, was written to the king's satraps and to the governors over all the provinces and to the officials of all the peoples, to every province in its own script and every people in its own language. It was written in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed with the king's signet ring. Letters were sent by couriers to all the king's provinces with instruction to destroy, to kill, and to annihilate all Jews, young and old, women and children, in one day, the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar, and to plunder their goods.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the king's scribes were summoned on the thirteenth day of the first month. The thirteenth of Nisan. The Passover lambs were killed on the fourteenth (Exod 12:6). The decree of death was written on the eve of Passover, and it would reach Jewish homes as they gathered to remember that God had once struck down the firstborn of their oppressors and spared theirs.

Letters were sent by couriers to all the king's provinces with instruction to destroy, to kill, and to annihilate all Jews, young and old, women and children, in one day, the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar, and to plunder their goods.

Three verbs, so that no one could misunderstand. And the list, young and old, women and children, is the list Saul was given against Amalek: kill both man and woman, child and infant (1 Sam 15:3). Saul did not carry out that sentence on Agag's people. Now an Agagite writes it against the people of Saul. The plunder was the bribe: whoever killed a Jew could keep his house. The same postal system that carried the letters about Vashti in chapter 1, to every province in its own script and every people in its own language, now carries a death sentence to every Jewish family from India to Ethiopia. Eleven months to wait for it.

verseByVerse.quote: A copy of the document was to be issued as a decree in every province by proclamation to all the peoples to be ready for that day. The couriers went out hurriedly by order of the king, and the decree was issued in Susa the citadel. And the king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was thrown into confusion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A copy of the document was to be issued as a decree in every province by proclamation to all the peoples to be ready for that day. The couriers went out hurriedly by order of the king, and the decree was issued in Susa the citadel. In every town in the empire it was nailed up for the neighbours to read: be ready.

And the king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was thrown into confusion.

One sentence, two scenes. Inside, two powerful men with their cups, business concluded. Outside, a city that did not understand what had just happened. Even pagan Susa was shaken by it. It is the picture of the powerful condemning the innocent and sitting down content. The Gospels have another such scene: when the innocent Son of God had been sent from one ruler to another, Herod and Pilate became friends with each other that very day (Luke 23:12), and at the foot of his cross the soldiers cast lots for his clothing (John 19:24).

But notice what the decree cannot do. It can name a day eleven months away. It cannot stop the One who governs every lot from working in those eleven months. The Jews of Susa went to bed that night under a law that could not be repealed. They did not yet know that a Jew was wearing the queen's crown, and that God had put her there five years before the danger existed.

4.title: For Such a Time as This: The Hinge of the Book
4.text: <sup>1</sup>When Mordecai learned all that had been done, Mordecai tore his clothes and put on sackcloth and ashes, and went out into the midst of the city, and he cried out with a loud and bitter cry.<sup>2</sup>He went up to the entrance of the king's gate, for no one was allowed to enter the king's gate clothed in sackcloth.<sup>3</sup>And in every province, wherever the king's command and his decree reached, there was great mourning among the Jews, with fasting and weeping and lamenting, and many of them lay in sackcloth and ashes.<sup>4</sup>When Esther's young women and her eunuchs came and told her, the queen was deeply distressed. She sent garments to clothe Mordecai, so that he might take off his sackcloth, but he would not accept them.<sup>5</sup>Then Esther called for Hathach, one of the king's eunuchs, who had been appointed to attend her, and ordered him to go to Mordecai to learn what this was and why it was.<sup>6</sup>Hathach went out to Mordecai in the open square of the city in front of the king's gate,<sup>7</sup>and Mordecai told him all that had happened to him, and the exact sum of money that Haman had promised to pay into the king's treasuries for the destruction of the Jews.<sup>8</sup>Mordecai also gave him a copy of the written decree issued in Susa for their destruction, that he might show it to Esther and explain it to her and command her to go to the king to beg his favor and plead with him on behalf of her people.<sup>9</sup>And Hathach went and told Esther what Mordecai had said.<sup>10</sup>Then Esther spoke to Hathach and commanded him to go to Mordecai and say,<sup>11</sup>"All the king's servants and the people of the king's provinces know that if any man or woman goes to the king inside the inner court without being called, there is but one law—to be put to death, except the one to whom the king holds out the golden scepter so that he may live. But as for me, I have not been called to come in to the king these thirty days."<sup>12</sup>And they told Mordecai what Esther had said.<sup>13</sup>Then Mordecai told them to reply to Esther, "Do not think to yourself that in the king's palace you will escape any more than all the other Jews.<sup>14</sup>For if you keep silent at this time, relief and deliverance will rise for the Jews from another place, but you and your father's house will perish. And who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?"<sup>15</sup>Then Esther told them to reply to Mordecai,<sup>16</sup>"Go, gather all the Jews to be found in Susa, and hold a fast on my behalf, and do not eat or drink for three days, night or day. I and my young women will also fast as you do. Then I will go to the king, though it is against the law, and if I perish, I perish."<sup>17</sup>Mordecai then went away and did everything as Esther had ordered him.
4.overview: When Mordecai learns of the decree he tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth and ashes and cries aloud through the city to the king's gate, and in every province the Jews mourn with fasting and weeping (vv. 1-3). Esther sends him clothes, which he refuses; through her eunuch Hathach he sends her the full story, the sum Haman offered, and a copy of the decree, and tells her to go and plead for her people (vv. 4-9). She answers that anyone who enters the king's inner court uncalled dies unless he holds out the golden sceptre, and she has not been called for thirty days (vv. 10-12). Mordecai replies that the palace will not save her; if she keeps silent, deliverance will come from another place, but she and her father's house will perish, and who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this? (vv. 13-14). Esther asks the Jews of Susa to fast three days for her, as she will: then I will go to the king, though it is against the law, and if I perish, I perish; and Mordecai does as she orders (vv. 15-17).
4.theology:
God's purpose to preserve his people is certain, and the people he places are still called to act; neither truth cancels the other. The chapter never names God and is full of him: sackcloth, fasting and the who knows of the prophets (Joel 2:14; Jonah 3:9) are the language of a people crying to the only one who can reverse a sentence.

Esther risks death to plead for a condemned people before a king whose law is death. Christ went knowing he would die, bore the sentence, and now holds the sceptre out to all who come through him (Luke 22:42; John 18:4; Heb 4:16).
4.examples:
Mordecai's great and bitter cry is Esau's cry, and Amalek was Esau's grandson.

No one could enter the king's gate in sackcloth.

Esther's first instinct was to send clothes.

Mordecai knew the exact sum of money.

Thirty days without being called.

Who knows: the words of Joel, and of the king of Nineveh in his ashes.

If I perish, I perish — three words in Hebrew.

The girl who had always obeyed Mordecai now gave him his orders.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — A Loud and Bitter Cry
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Mordecai tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth and ashes, and goes through the city with a loud and bitter cry, as far as the king's gate, which no one may enter in sackcloth (vv. 1-2). In every province there is great mourning among the Jews, with fasting and weeping and lamenting (v. 3). Esther, deeply distressed, sends him clothes, which he refuses (v. 4). Through her eunuch Hathach he sends her the whole story, the exact sum Haman promised, and a copy of the decree, and tells her to go to the king to beg his favor and plead with him on behalf of her people (vv. 5-9).
verseByVerse.theology: The empire had a law that grief must stay outside the king's gate. A whole people in sackcloth, fasting, crying out — and in a book that never mentions prayer, it is impossible to read this as anything else.

verseByVerse.quote: When Mordecai learned all that had been done, Mordecai tore his clothes and put on sackcloth and ashes, and went out into the midst of the city, and he cried out with a loud and bitter cry. He went up to the entrance of the king's gate, for no one was allowed to enter the king's gate clothed in sackcloth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Mordecai learned all that had been done, Mordecai tore his clothes and put on sackcloth and ashes, and went out into the midst of the city, and he cried out with a loud and bitter cry.

Not a private grief. He goes into the middle of the city in sackcloth, ashes on his head, crying aloud. Everyone in Susa can see and hear what the king's decree means.

And the words the narrator chooses are old ones. A great and bitter cry is, in Hebrew, the cry of Esau when he found that Jacob had taken his father's blessing: he cried out with an exceedingly great and bitter cry (Gen 27:34). Amalek was Esau's grandson (Gen 36:12). Now an Agagite, of Amalek's line, has drawn the same cry out of a son of Jacob. The old family quarrel runs all the way to Susa.

He went up to the entrance of the king's gate, for no one was allowed to enter the king's gate clothed in sackcloth. The Persian palace had a rule: no grief inside. The king was not to be troubled by mourning. So Mordecai goes as far as he is allowed and cries at the door.

Set that beside the throne the Christian approaches. There, mourners are not kept at the gate; they are the ones Christ calls blessed: Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted (Matt 5:4). He came to give them a beautiful headdress instead of ashes, the oil of gladness instead of mourning (Isa 61:3). No one needs to change out of sackcloth to come to him.

verseByVerse.quote: And in every province, wherever the king's command and his decree reached, there was great mourning among the Jews, with fasting and weeping and lamenting, and many of them lay in sackcloth and ashes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And in every province, wherever the king's command and his decree reached, there was great mourning among the Jews, with fasting and weeping and lamenting, and many of them lay in sackcloth and ashes.

The couriers rode out to every province, and behind them, town after town, the Jews put on sackcloth. Picture a Jewish family in a village a thousand miles from Susa reading the notice on the wall: on a day in Adar, eleven months from now, your neighbours may kill you and keep your house.

And what do they do? Fasting and weeping and lamenting. Prayer is not mentioned; it does not need to be. Those are the words of Joel's call to a people under judgment: return to me with all your heart, with fasting, with weeping, and with mourning (Joel 2:12). The book never says they prayed. It shows a whole nation doing what people do when they have no one left to cry to except God.

verseByVerse.quote: When Esther's young women and her eunuchs came and told her, the queen was deeply distressed. She sent garments to clothe Mordecai, so that he might take off his sackcloth, but he would not accept them. Then Esther called for Hathach, one of the king's eunuchs, who had been appointed to attend her, and ordered him to go to Mordecai to learn what this was and why it was. Hathach went out to Mordecai in the open square of the city in front of the king's gate,
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Esther's young women and her eunuchs came and told her, the queen was deeply distressed. She sent garments to clothe Mordecai, so that he might take off his sackcloth, but he would not accept them.

Esther does not yet know about the decree. She only knows that Mordecai is in sackcloth at the gate, and her first instinct is to get him into proper clothes. It is a very human instinct: fix the outside, and perhaps the trouble will go away. He will not have it. The sackcloth is the message. As Joel said, the point is to rend your hearts and not your garments (Joel 2:13), and no change of clothes can deal with a decree of death.

Then Esther called for Hathach, one of the king's eunuchs, who had been appointed to attend her, and ordered him to go to Mordecai to learn what this was and why it was. From here the whole conversation passes through a go-between. The queen cannot go out; Mordecai cannot come in. Every word between them is carried across the palace courtyard by a servant.

verseByVerse.quote: and Mordecai told him all that had happened to him, and the exact sum of money that Haman had promised to pay into the king's treasuries for the destruction of the Jews. Mordecai also gave him a copy of the written decree issued in Susa for their destruction, that he might show it to Esther and explain it to her and command her to go to the king to beg his favor and plead with him on behalf of her people. And Hathach went and told Esther what Mordecai had said.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Mordecai told him all that had happened to him, and the exact sum of money that Haman had promised to pay into the king's treasuries for the destruction of the Jews. The exact sum. Mordecai knew the ten thousand talents (3:9); a man at the king's gate hears things. He wants Esther to know exactly what her people are worth to Haman.

Mordecai also gave him a copy of the written decree issued in Susa for their destruction, that he might show it to Esther and explain it to her and command her to go to the king to beg his favor and plead with him on behalf of her people.

Her people. For years Mordecai had told her to keep her people secret (2:10, 20). Now he tells her to go in and plead for them. The secret that protected her has become the thing she must risk. And the word plead is the language of intercession: a queen standing between a king and a condemned people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–14 — For Such a Time as This
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Esther replies that anyone who goes to the king uncalled is put to death unless he holds out the golden sceptre. But as for me, I have not been called to come in to the king these thirty days (vv. 10-12). Mordecai answers: Do not think to yourself that in the king's palace you will escape any more than all the other Jews. For if you keep silent at this time, relief and deliverance will rise for the Jews from another place, but you and your father's house will perish. And who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this? (vv. 13-14).
verseByVerse.theology: Two convictions in one breath: God's people will be delivered whatever Esther does; and Esther is where she is for a reason. Neither cancels the other. God does not need her, and he has placed her.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Esther spoke to Hathach and commanded him to go to Mordecai and say, "All the king's servants and the people of the king's provinces know that if any man or woman goes to the king inside the inner court without being called, there is but one law—to be put to death, except the one to whom the king holds out the golden scepter so that he may live. But as for me, I have not been called to come in to the king these thirty days." And they told Mordecai what Esther had said.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All the king's servants and the people of the king's provinces know that if any man or woman goes to the king inside the inner court without being called, there is but one law — to be put to death, except the one to whom the king holds out the golden scepter so that he may live.

Esther is not making excuses. She is telling Mordecai the truth about the palace. Everyone knows the law. To walk into the inner court uncalled is to walk into your own execution, unless the king, in that moment, chooses to lift his golden sceptre toward you.

But as for me, I have not been called to come in to the king these thirty days. And that is the frightening part. Thirty days, and no summons. The harem had gone on filling after she was crowned (2:19). She has no reason to think the king still wants to see her, and every reason to remember what happened to the last queen who crossed him. The crown on her head does not make her safe.

Many readers know the feeling: knowing what ought to be done and knowing exactly what it may cost. Esther's hesitation is not cowardice. It is honesty about the price, and that is where real courage has to start.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Mordecai told them to reply to Esther, "Do not think to yourself that in the king's palace you will escape any more than all the other Jews.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Mordecai told them to reply to Esther, Do not think to yourself that in the king's palace you will escape any more than all the other Jews.

Mordecai takes away her last hiding place. The decree says all Jews. The palace walls will not stop it, and sooner or later someone will tell Haman who the queen's cousin is. Silence will not save her. It will only mean that she dies later, having done nothing.

That is still the truth about silence. A believer who hides in a comfortable place while the people of God are in danger may keep his comfort for a while. He has not escaped.

verseByVerse.quote: For if you keep silent at this time, relief and deliverance will rise for the Jews from another place, but you and your father's house will perish. And who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if you keep silent at this time, relief and deliverance will rise for the Jews from another place, but you and your father's house will perish. And who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?

Two things, and both are true. First: relief and deliverance will rise for the Jews from another place. Mordecai is sure the people will survive. He does not say how. God had sworn that Israel would last as long as the sun and moon (Jer 31:35-36), and centuries later another Benjaminite would ask, has God rejected his people? By no means! (Rom 11:1). Later Jewish writers used the Place as a name for God, and some hear it here; whether or not that is meant, the conviction is that the deliverance does not depend on Esther.

And you and your father's house will perish. Her father's name has been given only once, when she went in to the king: Esther the daughter of Abihail (2:15). As far as we are told, she is all that is left of that house. If she hides, the line ends with her.
