Second: who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this? An orphan made queen. Crowned five years before anyone had heard of Haman's plan. Mordecai looks at the strange road that brought her to the throne and asks whether this was what it was for.

And notice the words who knows. They are the words of the prophets calling a people under sentence to repent: Who knows whether he will not turn and relent (Joel 2:14). And they are the words of the king of Nineveh, sitting in ashes, ordering a fast and sackcloth: Who knows? God may turn and relent and turn from his fierce anger, so that we may not perish (Jonah 3:9). Sackcloth, ashes, fasting, who knows, perish: every one of them is in this chapter. The name of God is not, but the reader of the prophets can hear exactly whom they are hoping in.

Here is a question every believer can put to himself. Where has God put you — which family, which job, which friendships, which room you can walk into that others cannot? It is not an accident. There may be a moment for which it was all arranged, and you may be the only one in a position to speak.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–17 — If I Perish, I Perish
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Go, gather all the Jews to be found in Susa, and hold a fast on my behalf, and do not eat or drink for three days, night or day. I and my young women will also fast as you do. Then I will go to the king, though it is against the law, and if I perish, I perish (vv. 15-16). Mordecai then went away and did everything as Esther had ordered him (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: The orphan who once did whatever Mordecai told her (2:20) now gives the orders. She goes to the throne not knowing whether she will live. There is a greater intercessor who went knowing he would die (John 18:4).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Esther told them to reply to Mordecai, "Go, gather all the Jews to be found in Susa, and hold a fast on my behalf, and do not eat or drink for three days, night or day. I and my young women will also fast as you do. Then I will go to the king, though it is against the law, and if I perish, I perish."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Esther told them to reply to Mordecai, Go, gather all the Jews to be found in Susa, and hold a fast on my behalf, and do not eat or drink for three days, night or day. I and my young women will also fast as you do.

She does not go alone. She asks her people to fast for her, and she and her maids will fast with them. Three days without food or water, the whole Jewish community of Susa and a queen's household together. It is prayer in everything but the word. And if the fast began as soon as the news came, it fell across the days of Passover, for the decree had been written on the eve of that feast (3:12). The Jews of Susa may have spent the Passover of that year not eating the lamb but fasting.

Then I will go to the king, though it is against the law, and if I perish, I perish.

In Hebrew it is three words. Not: I will not perish, which would be bravado. Not: I hope I will not perish, which would be wishful thinking. If I perish, I perish. She will go, and what happens is not in her hands. That is the shape of courage for a believer: not certainty of the outcome, but willingness to act and leave the outcome with God.

Though it is against the law. She knows she is breaking the king's law, and she does it deliberately, because keeping it would mean standing by while her people were killed. Scripture honours that kind of disobedience: Moses' parents hid their baby and they were not afraid of the king's edict (Heb 11:23). A believer may have to break a human rule to keep a greater duty. What he may not do is pretend that the rule does not exist; Esther names it, and pays the price of breaking it in advance.

And it points to a greater scene. In a garden outside Jerusalem another intercessor faced the cost of standing for his people and prayed, not my will, but yours, be done (Luke 22:42). Esther went in not knowing whether she would die. Jesus went knowing all that would happen to him (John 18:4), and he did die, under the sentence that was ours. That is why, for those who belong to him, the sceptre is always held out: Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace (Heb 4:16).

verseByVerse.quote: Mordecai then went away and did everything as Esther had ordered him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mordecai then went away and did everything as Esther had ordered him.

A small sentence, and a reversal. In chapter 2 Esther obeyed Mordecai just as when she was brought up by him (2:20). Now the girl he raised gives the orders, and he carries them out. The orphan has become the one her people depend on. Something has changed in her in the space of this chapter, and from here to the end of the book it is Esther who leads.

5.title: The First Banquet: Grace, Delay, and the Gallows
5.text: <sup>1</sup>On the third day Esther put on her royal robes and stood in the inner court of the king's palace, in front of the king's quarters, while the king was sitting on his royal throne inside the throne room opposite the entrance to the palace.<sup>2</sup>And when the king saw Queen Esther standing in the court, she won favor in his sight, and he held out to Esther the golden scepter that was in his hand. Then Esther approached and touched the tip of the scepter.<sup>3</sup>And the king said to her, "What is it, Queen Esther? What is your request? It shall be given you, even to the half of my kingdom."<sup>4</sup>And Esther said, "If it please the king, let the king and Haman come today to a feast that I have prepared for the king."<sup>5</sup>Then the king said, "Bring Haman quickly, so that we may do as Esther has asked." So the king and Haman came to the feast that Esther had prepared.<sup>6</sup>And as they were drinking wine after the feast, the king said to Esther, "What is your wish? It shall be granted you. And what is your request? Even to the half of my kingdom, it shall be fulfilled."<sup>7</sup>Then Esther answered, "My wish and my request is:<sup>8</sup>If I have found favor in the sight of the king, and if it please the king to grant my wish and fulfill my request, let the king and Haman come to the feast that I will prepare for them, and tomorrow I will do as the king has said."<sup>9</sup>And Haman went out that day joyful and glad of heart. But when Haman saw Mordecai in the king's gate, that he neither rose nor trembled before him, he was filled with wrath against Mordecai.<sup>10</sup>Nevertheless, Haman restrained himself and went home, and he sent and brought his friends and his wife Zeresh.<sup>11</sup>And Haman recounted to them the splendor of his riches, the number of his sons, all the promotions with which the king had honored him, and how he had advanced him above the officials and the servants of the king.<sup>12</sup>Then Haman said, "Even Queen Esther let no one but me come with the king to the feast she prepared. And tomorrow also I am invited by her together with the king.<sup>13</sup>Yet all this is worth nothing to me, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate."<sup>14</sup>Then his wife Zeresh and all his friends said to him, "Let a gallows fifty cubits high be made, and in the morning tell the king to have Mordecai hanged upon it. Then go joyfully with the king to the feast." This idea pleased Haman, and he had the gallows made.
5.overview: On the third day of the fast Esther puts on her royal robes and stands in the inner court; the king sees her, holds out the golden sceptre, and she touches it and lives (vv. 1-2). Offered anything up to half the kingdom, she asks only that the king and Haman come to a feast she has prepared (vv. 3-5). Over the wine he asks again, and she begins to answer and then invites them to a second feast the next day (vv. 6-8). Haman leaves delighted, but sees Mordecai at the gate refusing to rise or tremble and is filled with fury (vv. 9-10). At home he recounts his riches, sons, honours and the queen's invitation, and says it is all worth nothing while Mordecai sits at the gate; Zeresh and his friends advise a gallows fifty cubits high for Mordecai in the morning, and he has it built (vv. 11-14).
5.theology:
Grace at the throne: Esther approaches uncalled and is received. God works through her courage and through her delay; the extra night she creates is the night he will use. Pride, meanwhile, counts everything as nothing for want of one man's bow, and builds the instrument of its own destruction (Prov 16:18).

The sceptre held out to Esther is held out for good to all who come through Christ (Heb 4:16). The tree raised for a righteous Jew anticipates the tree on which the righteous One bore the sins of the guilty (Acts 5:30; 1 Pet 2:24).
5.examples:
From sackcloth to royal robes.

She had prepared the feast before she went in.

Half of my kingdom: Herod's offer bought the Baptist's head; Esther's would buy lives.

My wish and my request is — and then another invitation.

Mordecai neither rose nor trembled.

Everything minus one man's bow came to nothing for Haman.

A gallows seventy-five feet high, built through the night the king could not sleep.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the third day Esther puts on her royal robes and stands in the inner court, and when the king saw Queen Esther standing in the court, she won favor in his sight, and he held out to Esther the golden scepter (vv. 1-2). What is your request? It shall be given you, even to the half of my kingdom (v. 3). She asks only that the king and Haman come to a feast (vv. 4-5). Over the wine he asks again; she begins to answer, and instead invites them both to a second feast tomorrow (vv. 6-8).
verseByVerse.theology: She went in under the sentence of death and lived. And then she did not ask. The one extra night that her delay created is the night on which the whole story turns (6:1).

verseByVerse.quote: On the third day Esther put on her royal robes and stood in the inner court of the king's palace, in front of the king's quarters, while the king was sitting on his royal throne inside the throne room opposite the entrance to the palace. And when the king saw Queen Esther standing in the court, she won favor in his sight, and he held out to Esther the golden scepter that was in his hand. Then Esther approached and touched the tip of the scepter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the third day Esther put on her royal robes and stood in the inner court of the king's palace, in front of the king's quarters, while the king was sitting on his royal throne inside the throne room opposite the entrance to the palace.

The third day of the fast. She has not eaten or drunk for three days. She takes off whatever she fasted in and puts on her royal robes: she will go to the king as the queen, not as a beggar. And she stands where he can see her, in the court facing the open throne room, and waits for his eyes to fall on her. One look will decide whether she lives.

Third days in Scripture are often days of deliverance. On the third day Abraham saw the mountain where God would provide the lamb (Gen 22:4); on the third day he will raise us up, said Hosea (Hos 6:2). The Christian reader knows the third day on which the one under the sentence of death came out alive (1 Cor 15:4). Esther's third day is a small one, and it points the same way.

And when the king saw Queen Esther standing in the court, she won favor in his sight, and he held out to Esther the golden scepter that was in his hand. Then Esther approached and touched the tip of the scepter. The sceptre comes up; she crosses the floor and touches it; she will live. It is the most dangerous walk in the book, and it takes one sentence. For those who belong to Christ, that walk has been made safe for good: Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace (Heb 4:16).

verseByVerse.quote: And the king said to her, "What is it, Queen Esther? What is your request? It shall be given you, even to the half of my kingdom." And Esther said, "If it please the king, let the king and Haman come today to a feast that I have prepared for the king."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the king said to her, What is it, Queen Esther? What is your request? It shall be given you, even to the half of my kingdom. He knows she would not risk her life for nothing. Half of my kingdom is the royal way of saying: ask anything. Another king used the same words five centuries later: Herod, at his birthday feast, promised a dancing girl up to half of my kingdom (Mark 6:23), and she asked for the head of John the Baptist. Esther will use the same offer to ask for lives.

And Esther said, If it please the king, let the king and Haman come today to a feast that I have prepared for the king. Not a petition; an invitation. She had prepared the feast before she went in — she was planning to live. And she asks for Haman to be there. The man who wrote the decree will be at her table when she asks for it to be undone.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king said, "Bring Haman quickly, so that we may do as Esther has asked." So the king and Haman came to the feast that Esther had prepared. And as they were drinking wine after the feast, the king said to Esther, "What is your wish? It shall be granted you. And what is your request? Even to the half of my kingdom, it shall be fulfilled." Then Esther answered, "My wish and my request is: If I have found favor in the sight of the king, and if it please the king to grant my wish and fulfill my request, let the king and Haman come to the feast that I will prepare for them, and tomorrow I will do as the king has said."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the king said, Bring Haman quickly, so that we may do as Esther has asked. So the king and Haman came to the feast that Esther had prepared. The king, the queen, and the enemy of the Jews, drinking together. Only one of the three knows what is at stake.

And as they were drinking wine after the feast, the king said to Esther, What is your wish? It shall be granted you. And what is your request? Even to the half of my kingdom, it shall be fulfilled. The second time of asking. The moment has come.

Then Esther answered, My wish and my request is: If I have found favor in the sight of the king, and if it please the king to grant my wish and fulfill my request, let the king and Haman come to the feast that I will prepare for them, and tomorrow I will do as the king has said.

Watch the sentence. She begins, My wish and my request is — and then it becomes another invitation. Did her courage fail at the last moment? Did she judge that the king was not ready, or that one more feast would bind him to her more tightly? The narrator does not say. What he shows us is that the delay gave God one night to work with, and that he used it. Many readers know what it is to have meant to say the hard thing and not said it yet. Delay is not always failure. The question is whether you go back tomorrow. Esther did.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–14 — Let a Gallows Fifty Cubits High Be Made
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Haman leaves joyful and glad of heart, sees Mordecai at the gate refusing to rise or tremble, and is filled with wrath (v. 9). At home he lists his riches, his sons, his honours and the queen's invitation, and says of it all: worth nothing to me, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate (vv. 10-13). His wife Zeresh and his friends advise a gallows fifty cubits high for Mordecai in the morning, and a joyful feast afterwards; this idea pleased Haman, and he had the gallows made (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: Everything he had, minus one man's bow, came to nothing. That is pride's arithmetic. And the tree he raised that night for a righteous Jew will stand in the next chapter with a different body on it.

verseByVerse.quote: And Haman went out that day joyful and glad of heart. But when Haman saw Mordecai in the king's gate, that he neither rose nor trembled before him, he was filled with wrath against Mordecai. Nevertheless, Haman restrained himself and went home, and he sent and brought his friends and his wife Zeresh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Haman went out that day joyful and glad of heart. But when Haman saw Mordecai in the king's gate, that he neither rose nor trembled before him, he was filled with wrath against Mordecai. One sentence takes him from delight to fury. He has dined privately with the king and queen, and one man at the gate who will not stand up for him ruins the whole day. Neither rose nor trembled: Mordecai, under a sentence of death, is not afraid of him.

Nevertheless, Haman restrained himself and went home, and he sent and brought his friends and his wife Zeresh. He controls his face in public and goes home to talk about it. That is how grudges grow.

verseByVerse.quote: And Haman recounted to them the splendor of his riches, the number of his sons, all the promotions with which the king had honored him, and how he had advanced him above the officials and the servants of the king. Then Haman said, "Even Queen Esther let no one but me come with the king to the feast she prepared. And tomorrow also I am invited by her together with the king. Yet all this is worth nothing to me, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Haman recounted to them the splendor of his riches, the number of his sons, all the promotions with which the king had honored him, and how he had advanced him above the officials and the servants of the king. He tells his own wife and friends what they already know. Riches, ten sons (9:7-10), honours, rank. And the crowning boast: Even Queen Esther let no one but me come with the king to the feast she prepared. And tomorrow also I am invited by her together with the king. He thinks the invitation is the height of his career. It is the trap.

Yet all this, he says, is worth nothing to me, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate.

Everything, minus one man's bow, equals nothing. That is the arithmetic of pride, and it never comes out. There will always be one person who does not bow. Here is a test to run on ourselves: is there one person whose coolness, or success, or refusal to give me my due, spoils everything else I have? If so, the problem is not that person.

Set Haman's sentence beside Paul's. I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord (Phil 3:8). Both men count everything as nothing because of one person. Haman, because of a man he hated; Paul, because of the One he loved. The first sentence leads to a gallows. The second leads to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Then his wife Zeresh and all his friends said to him, "Let a gallows fifty cubits high be made, and in the morning tell the king to have Mordecai hanged upon it. Then go joyfully with the king to the feast." This idea pleased Haman, and he had the gallows made.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then his wife Zeresh and all his friends said to him, Let a gallows fifty cubits high be made, and in the morning tell the king to have Mordecai hanged upon it. Then go joyfully with the king to the feast. This idea pleased Haman, and he had the gallows made.

Fifty cubits is about seventy-five feet. The word is simply a tree or a stake, and this one would stand higher than the houses, so that all Susa could see what happened to a Jew who would not bow. Kill Mordecai before breakfast, then enjoy the queen's dinner. This idea pleased Haman: the book's favourite phrase, and this time it pleases the one man it should have frightened. Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall (Prov 16:18).

The carpenters worked through the night. It was the night the king could not sleep (6:1). And a reader of the whole Bible cannot see a tree raised to kill a righteous Jew without thinking of another: Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree (Acts 5:30). Haman's tree would be turned against the guilty. Christ's tree was the one on which the Innocent bore our sins in his body (1 Pet 2:24).

6.title: The Night the King Could Not Sleep
6.text: <sup>1</sup>On that night the king could not sleep. And he gave orders to bring the book of memorable deeds, the chronicles, and they were read before the king.<sup>2</sup>And it was found written how Mordecai had told about Bigthana and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs, who guarded the threshold, and who had sought to lay hands on King Ahasuerus.<sup>3</sup>And the king said, "What honor or distinction has been bestowed on Mordecai for this?" The king's young men who attended him said, "Nothing has been done for him."<sup>4</sup>And the king said, "Who is in the court?" Now Haman had just entered the outer court of the king's palace to speak to the king about having Mordecai hanged on the gallows that he had prepared for him.<sup>5</sup>And the king's young men told him, "Haman is there, standing in the court." And the king said, "Let him come in."<sup>6</sup>So Haman came in, and the king said to him, "What should be done to the man whom the king delights to honor?" And Haman said to himself, "Whom would the king delight to honor more than me?"<sup>7</sup>And Haman said to the king, "For the man whom the king delights to honor,<sup>8</sup>let royal robes be brought, which the king has worn, and the horse that the king has ridden, and on whose head a royal crown is set.<sup>9</sup>And let the robes and the horse be handed over to one of the king's most noble officials. Let them dress the man whom the king delights to honor, and let them lead him on the horse through the square of the city, proclaiming before him: 'Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delights to honor.'"<sup>10</sup>Then the king said to Haman, "Hurry; take the robes and the horse, as you have said, and do so to Mordecai the Jew, who sits at the king's gate. Leave out nothing that you have mentioned."<sup>11</sup>So Haman took the robes and the horse, and he dressed Mordecai and led him through the square of the city, proclaiming before him, "Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delights to honor."<sup>12</sup>Then Mordecai returned to the king's gate. But Haman hurried to his house, mourning and with his head covered.<sup>13</sup>And Haman told his wife Zeresh and all his friends everything that had happened to him. Then his wise men and his wife Zeresh said to him, "If Mordecai, before whom you have begun to fall, is of the Jewish people, you will not overcome him but will surely fall before him."<sup>14</sup>While they were yet talking with him, the king's eunuchs arrived and hurried to bring Haman to the feast that Esther had prepared.
6.overview: That night the king cannot sleep and has the royal chronicles read to him; they reach the record of Mordecai's exposure of the plot against his life, and he learns that nothing was ever done for him (vv. 1-3). At dawn Haman arrives to ask for Mordecai's hanging, and the king asks him what should be done for the man whom the king delights to honor (vv. 4-6). Thinking it can only be himself, Haman proposes the king's robes and horse and a public proclamation (vv. 7-9), and is ordered to do all of it for Mordecai the Jew, which he does, leading him through the city square (vv. 10-11). Mordecai returns to the gate; Haman hurries home mourning with his head covered, and his wife and wise men tell him that if Mordecai is a Jew, he will surely fall before him (vv. 12-13). The king's eunuchs arrive to hurry him to Esther's feast (v. 14).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — On That Night the King Could Not Sleep
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On that night the king could not sleep. And he gave orders to bring the book of memorable deeds, the chronicles, and they were read before the king (v. 1). The reading reaches the record of how Mordecai exposed the plot against the king's life (v. 2). What honor or distinction has been bestowed on Mordecai for this? Nothing has been done for him (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The gallows was going up across the city, the queen's second feast was hours away, and the king could not sleep. Of all the pages in the royal annals, the one that was read was the one about Mordecai. The book never says who kept the king awake.

verseByVerse.quote: On that night the king could not sleep. And he gave orders to bring the book of memorable deeds, the chronicles, and they were read before the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On that night the king could not sleep.

That night: the night after Esther's first feast, the night Haman's carpenters were raising a gallows seventy-five feet high. Literally, the king's sleep fled. Almost the same words are used, in the Aramaic of Daniel, of another Persian-era king on another night when a Jew's life hung in the balance: Darius, with Daniel in the lions' den, spent the night fasting ... and sleep fled from him (Dan 6:18).

Who took the king's sleep? The Hebrew text does not say. When the book was translated into Greek, the translators could not bear the silence and wrote that the Lord took sleep from the king. The Hebrew leaves it unsaid, and trusts the reader. We are not told, and we know. Behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep (Ps 121:4). The emperor of the world lay awake that night because the Keeper of Israel was awake.

And he gave orders to bring the book of memorable deeds, the chronicles, and they were read before the king. A cure for insomnia: have the court records read aloud. The book's name is, literally, the book of remembrances. The deed filed and forgotten in 2:23 is in it. Malachi spoke of another such book: a book of remembrance was written before him of those who feared the LORD (Mal 3:16).

Many readers have lain awake at night with something that will not leave them. The king's sleepless night was not wasted. Neither are ours. The One who does not sleep uses the hours we cannot.

verseByVerse.quote: And it was found written how Mordecai had told about Bigthana and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs, who guarded the threshold, and who had sought to lay hands on King Ahasuerus. And the king said, "What honor or distinction has been bestowed on Mordecai for this?" The king's young men who attended him said, "Nothing has been done for him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And it was found written how Mordecai had told about Bigthana and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs, who guarded the threshold, and who had sought to lay hands on King Ahasuerus. Years of records from 127 provinces, and the reader happened to reach this page. It was found written. Nobody went looking for it.

And the king said, What honor or distinction has been bestowed on Mordecai for this? The king's young men who attended him said, Nothing has been done for him.

Nothing. The plot was uncovered some time after Esther became queen in the seventh year (2:16, 21); we are now in the twelfth (3:7). For something like five years the man who saved the king's life had received nothing. And the reward was delayed until the one morning in all those years when it would do the most good: the morning Haman came to ask for his death.

Take that quietly into your own life. Faithfulness that went unthanked is not lost. God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love that you have shown for his name (Heb 6:10). The reward may be years in coming, and it will come at the right time.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–11 — The Man Whom the King Delights to Honor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At that moment Haman arrives to ask for Mordecai's hanging (vv. 4-5). The king asks him, What should be done to the man whom the king delights to honor?, and Haman, thinking it must be himself, proposes the king's own robes, the king's own horse, and a noble to lead him through the city proclaiming his honour (vv. 6-9). Hurry; take the robes and the horse, as you have said, and do so to Mordecai the Jew (v. 10). Haman does it, proclaiming before him through the square (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: Haman designed the honour for himself and carried it out for the man he had come to kill. The gallows was ready; he spent the morning leading Mordecai's horse.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king said, "Who is in the court?" Now Haman had just entered the outer court of the king's palace to speak to the king about having Mordecai hanged on the gallows that he had prepared for him. And the king's young men told him, "Haman is there, standing in the court." And the king said, "Let him come in."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the king said, Who is in the court? Now Haman had just entered the outer court of the king's palace to speak to the king about having Mordecai hanged on the gallows that he had prepared for him.

The king has been awake all night thinking about how to honour Mordecai. Haman has been awake all night thinking about how to kill him. Both men converge on the throne room at dawn. Haman has come early because he is eager: the gallows is finished, and he wants the permission signed before Esther's feast. Of all the people who might have been waiting in the court at that hour, it is Haman.

And the king's young men told him, Haman is there, standing in the court. And the king said, Let him come in. He walks in with Mordecai's death in his mouth. He never gets to say it.

verseByVerse.quote: So Haman came in, and the king said to him, "What should be done to the man whom the king delights to honor?" And Haman said to himself, "Whom would the king delight to honor more than me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Haman came in, and the king said to him, What should be done to the man whom the king delights to honor? And Haman said to himself, Whom would the king delight to honor more than me?

The narrator lets us hear Haman's thought, and it is the whole man in eight words. It does not cross his mind that anyone else in the empire might be meant. In the world of the proud there is only one person who deserves honour.

Jesus told a story about a man like this at a wedding feast, who took the place of honour and was moved down to the lowest seat in front of everyone: everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 14:11). Haman is about to live out that sentence in the streets of Susa, and Mordecai the second half of it.

verseByVerse.quote: And Haman said to the king, "For the man whom the king delights to honor, let royal robes be brought, which the king has worn, and the horse that the king has ridden, and on whose head a royal crown is set. And let the robes and the horse be handed over to one of the king's most noble officials. Let them dress the man whom the king delights to honor, and let them lead him on the horse through the square of the city, proclaiming before him: 'Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delights to honor.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the man whom the king delights to honor, let royal robes be brought, which the king has worn, and the horse that the king has ridden, and on whose head a royal crown is set. Not money, not land. He wants to be seen wearing the king: the king's own clothes, on the king's own horse with the royal crest on its head. What Haman craved was not wealth, which he had, but to be treated as royalty in public.

And let the robes and the horse be handed over to one of the king's most noble officials. Let them dress the man whom the king delights to honor, and let them lead him on the horse through the square of the city, proclaiming before him: Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delights to honor. He has designed every detail, including the noble who will lead the horse. He has just written his own job for the worst morning of his life.

A reader of Genesis knows this scene. When Pharaoh raised Joseph, the Hebrew prisoner, he clothed him in garments of fine linen, set him in his chariot, and they called out before him, Bow the knee! (Gen 41:42-43). Another exile in a foreign court, lifted up by a king's robe and a public proclamation.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king said to Haman, "Hurry; take the robes and the horse, as you have said, and do so to Mordecai the Jew, who sits at the king's gate. Leave out nothing that you have mentioned." So Haman took the robes and the horse, and he dressed Mordecai and led him through the square of the city, proclaiming before him, "Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delights to honor."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the king said to Haman, Hurry; take the robes and the horse, as you have said, and do so to Mordecai the Jew, who sits at the king's gate. Leave out nothing that you have mentioned.

Every phrase lands. Mordecai. The Jew. Who sits at the king's gate — the very place where he had refused to bow. Leave out nothing. And notice that the king calls him Mordecai the Jew without a flicker. The decree he signed to kill all the Jews is still posted in every province, and the king has not connected the two. He honours a Jew in the morning under a law that will kill him in Adar.

So Haman took the robes and the horse, and he dressed Mordecai and led him through the square of the city, proclaiming before him, Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delights to honor. Haman dresses him with his own hands. Haman walks at the horse's head. Haman shouts the proclamation he had written for himself. The whole city sees it.

The man whom the king delights to honor. There is a King who delights to honour. At the Jordan his voice said of his Son, This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased (Matt 3:17), and after the cross God has highly exalted him (Phil 2:9). And that King's delight reaches those who belong to his Son: If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him (John 12:26). The servant who was overlooked will be dressed in robes not his own and brought through the city.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–14 — You Will Surely Fall Before Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Mordecai returns to the king's gate; Haman hurries home mourning and with his head covered (v. 12). His wise men and his wife say, If Mordecai, before whom you have begun to fall, is of the Jewish people, you will not overcome him but will surely fall before him (v. 13). While they are still talking, the king's eunuchs come to hurry him to Esther's feast (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: One of the plainest statements in the book that the Jews cannot be overcome comes from Haman's own household. Even his wife can see which way the story is going.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Mordecai returned to the king's gate. But Haman hurried to his house, mourning and with his head covered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Mordecai returned to the king's gate. The procession ends and he goes back to work. The honour has not gone to his head, and it has not changed his situation: the decree still stands. He returns to his post, as the faithful do.

But Haman hurried to his house, mourning and with his head covered. Covering the head was the gesture of grief and shame; David went up the Mount of Olives weeping as he went, barefoot and with his head covered (2 Sam 15:30). In chapter 4 it was Mordecai who mourned in the streets. Now the mourning has moved house. Haman walks home hiding his face.

verseByVerse.quote: And Haman told his wife Zeresh and all his friends everything that had happened to him. Then his wise men and his wife Zeresh said to him, "If Mordecai, before whom you have begun to fall, is of the Jewish people, you will not overcome him but will surely fall before him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Haman told his wife Zeresh and all his friends everything that had happened to him. Then his wise men and his wife Zeresh said to him, If Mordecai, before whom you have begun to fall, is of the Jewish people, you will not overcome him but will surely fall before him.

The night before, these same people had advised the gallows. This morning they deliver a verdict. And it is remarkable who says it. In a book that never names God, one of the clearest statements that the Jews cannot be destroyed comes from the enemy's own wife and advisers. They knew the history. God had said to Abraham, I will bless those who bless you, and him who dishonors you I will curse (Gen 12:3), and even Persian wise men had noticed that people who set themselves against this nation fell.

Begun to fall ... surely fall. The word comes twice. In the next chapter it will come a third time, when Haman is found falling on the couch where Esther lay (7:8).

verseByVerse.quote: While they were yet talking with him, the king's eunuchs arrived and hurried to bring Haman to the feast that Esther had prepared.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While they were yet talking with him, the king's eunuchs arrived and hurried to bring Haman to the feast that Esther had prepared.

No time to think, to plan, to recover. Hurry, said the king (v. 10); Haman hurried home (v. 12); now the eunuchs hurried him to the feast. The whole chapter has been one long morning that will not let him stop. He had been invited as the queen's honoured guest. He goes to her table with the words of his wife still in his ears.

That is how the book shows God's hand: not by naming him, but by the sheer timing. A sleepless night, a page found by chance, a man in the court at the wrong moment. Any one of them could be luck. All of them together, on the one night that mattered, make the reader say what the book never says. The Keeper of Israel had not been asleep.

6.theology:
God is unnamed and unmistakable: a king's sleep taken, a page found, a man in the court at the wrong moment, all on the one night that mattered. He who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep (Ps 121:4). Faithfulness left unrewarded for years is remembered at the right time (Heb 6:10).

The one who exalts himself is humbled and the humble is exalted (Luke 14:11). The King who delights to honour his Son (Matt 3:17; Phil 2:9) honours those who serve him (John 12:26).
6.examples:
The king's sleep fled; the Greek translators added the Lord, the Hebrew did not.

Out of years of records, the page about Mordecai.

Nothing has been done for him — for some five years.

Haman came to ask for a hanging and was asked to plan an honour.

He designed the honour for himself and led the horse for Mordecai.

The king honoured Mordecai the Jew under a decree to kill the Jews.

Haman's own wife said he would fall.

7.title: The Second Banquet: Esther Speaks, Haman Falls
7.text: <sup>1</sup>So the king and Haman went in to feast with Queen Esther.<sup>2</sup>And on the second day, as they were drinking wine after the feast, the king again said to Esther, "What is your wish, Queen Esther? It shall be granted you. And what is your request? Even to the half of my kingdom, it shall be fulfilled."<sup>3</sup>Then Queen Esther answered, "If I have found favor in your sight, O king, and if it please the king, let my life be granted me for my wish, and my people for my request.<sup>4</sup>For we have been sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, to be killed, and to be annihilated. If we had been sold merely as slaves, men and women, I would have been silent, for our affliction is not to be compared with the loss to the king."<sup>5</sup>Then King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther, "Who is he, and where is he, who has dared to do this?"<sup>6</sup>And Esther said, "A foe and enemy! This wicked Haman!" Then Haman was terrified before the king and the queen.<sup>7</sup>And the king arose in his wrath from the wine-drinking and went into the palace garden, but Haman stayed to beg for his life from Queen Esther, for he saw that harm was determined against him by the king.<sup>8</sup>And the king returned from the palace garden to the place where they were drinking wine, as Haman was falling on the couch where Esther was. And the king said, "Will he even assault the queen in my presence, in my own house?" As the word left the mouth of the king, they covered Haman's face.<sup>9</sup>Then Harbona, one of the eunuchs in attendance on the king, said, "Moreover, the gallows that Haman has prepared for Mordecai, whose word saved the king, is standing at Haman's house, fifty cubits high." And the king said, "Hang him on that."<sup>10</sup>So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Then the wrath of the king abated.
7.overview: At the second feast the king asks a third time for Esther's request (vv. 1-2). She asks for her life and her people's: we have been sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, to be killed, and to be annihilated, the words of the decree itself (vv. 3-4). When the king demands who has dared to do this, she points across the table: A foe and enemy! This wicked Haman! (vv. 5-6). The king goes out into the garden in fury; Haman stays to beg Esther for his life and is found falling on her couch, and his face is covered (vv. 7-8). The eunuch Harbona mentions the fifty-cubit gallows built for Mordecai, the man whose word saved the king, and the king orders Haman hanged on it; the king's wrath abates (vv. 9-10). But the decree still stands.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the second feast the king asks a third time what Esther wants (vv. 1-2). Let my life be granted me for my wish, and my people for my request. For we have been sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, to be killed, and to be annihilated (vv. 3-4). Who is he, and where is he, who has dared to do this? A foe and enemy! This wicked Haman! Then Haman was terrified before the king and the queen (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: The queen who had hidden her people for five years says I and my people in one breath, and names the man at the table. The king asks who dared to do what he himself had signed.

verseByVerse.quote: So the king and Haman went in to feast with Queen Esther. And on the second day, as they were drinking wine after the feast, the king again said to Esther, "What is your wish, Queen Esther? It shall be granted you. And what is your request? Even to the half of my kingdom, it shall be fulfilled."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the king and Haman went in to feast with Queen Esther. And on the second day, as they were drinking wine after the feast, the king again said to Esther, What is your wish, Queen Esther? It shall be granted you. And what is your request? Even to the half of my kingdom, it shall be fulfilled.

The third time of asking (5:3, 6). Haman is at the table: the same Haman who this morning led Mordecai's horse through the city and went home with his head covered, and whose wife told him he would fall. He has been hurried here with no time to think. The king is in good humour. The queen is gracious. Only she knows what she is about to say.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Queen Esther answered, "If I have found favor in your sight, O king, and if it please the king, let my life be granted me for my wish, and my people for my request. For we have been sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, to be killed, and to be annihilated. If we had been sold merely as slaves, men and women, I would have been silent, for our affliction is not to be compared with the loss to the king."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Queen Esther answered, If I have found favor in your sight, O king, and if it please the king, let my life be granted me for my wish, and my people for my request.

The king asked for her wish and her request. She gives him two answers in exactly that shape: my life, and my people. She puts herself first so that the king will feel it; the threat is to his own queen. And then, my people. The secret she has kept since the day she entered the harem (2:10) is given up in two words.

For we have been sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, to be killed, and to be annihilated. Those are the three verbs of Haman's decree, word for word (3:13). She quotes the king's own law back to him. And sold: someone paid for this. Ten thousand talents of silver (3:9). I and my people: she stands inside the sentence with them.

If we had been sold merely as slaves, men and women, I would have been silent, for our affliction is not to be compared with the loss to the king. Tact at the edge of death: she would not have troubled the king over mere slavery. But this is killing. It is the moment chapter 4 prayed for, and she speaks it with the courtesy of a queen and the courage of someone who has already said, if I perish, I perish.

verseByVerse.quote: Then King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther, "Who is he, and where is he, who has dared to do this?" And Esther said, "A foe and enemy! This wicked Haman!" Then Haman was terrified before the king and the queen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther, Who is he, and where is he, who has dared to do this?

The answer to the king's question is: you. He handed Haman the signet ring and said, the people also, to do with them as it seems good to you (3:11). He never asked which people. Now he asks who could have dared. It is a picture of how easily the powerful sign things and forget them, and how outraged they become when the thing they signed turns out to touch someone they love.

And Esther said, A foe and enemy! This wicked Haman! Then Haman was terrified before the king and the queen. After five years of silence and two days of feasts, she says his name, and she says it with him sitting there. The man who was filled with fury because a Jew would not tremble before him (5:9) trembles before a Jewish woman.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king storms out into the garden; Haman stays to beg Esther for his life (v. 7). The king returns to find him falling on the couch where Esther was, and they cover Haman's face (v. 8). The eunuch Harbona mentions the gallows fifty cubits high that Haman built for Mordecai, whose word saved the king. Hang him on that (v. 9). So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Then the wrath of the king abated (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: He makes a pit, digging it out, and falls into the hole that he has made (Ps 7:15). The tree Haman raised for a righteous man held the guilty one. At the cross it was the other way round.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king arose in his wrath from the wine-drinking and went into the palace garden, but Haman stayed to beg for his life from Queen Esther, for he saw that harm was determined against him by the king. And the king returned from the palace garden to the place where they were drinking wine, as Haman was falling on the couch where Esther was. And the king said, "Will he even assault the queen in my presence, in my own house?" As the word left the mouth of the king, they covered Haman's face.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the king arose in his wrath from the wine-drinking and went into the palace garden, but Haman stayed to beg for his life from Queen Esther, for he saw that harm was determined against him by the king. The king goes out into the night air. Perhaps he is furious; perhaps he is realising that the decree has his seal on it. Haman sees his death in the king's face, and does the one thing left: he begs. The man who required every knee at the gate to bend is on his knees before a Jew.

And the king returned from the palace garden to the place where they were drinking wine, as Haman was falling on the couch where Esther was. And the king said, Will he even assault the queen in my presence, in my own house? Guests reclined on couches to eat. Haman, pleading, throws himself down at the queen's couch just as the king walks back in. Falling: the word Zeresh used the day before, you will not overcome him but will surely fall before him (6:13). He falls, and it looks like the worst thing a man could do in the king's house.

As the word left the mouth of the king, they covered Haman's face. That morning Haman had covered his own head in shame (6:12). Now others cover it, and it means death.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Harbona, one of the eunuchs in attendance on the king, said, "Moreover, the gallows that Haman has prepared for Mordecai, whose word saved the king, is standing at Haman's house, fifty cubits high." And the king said, "Hang him on that."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Harbona, one of the eunuchs in attendance on the king, said, Moreover, the gallows that Haman has prepared for Mordecai, whose word saved the king, is standing at Haman's house, fifty cubits high.

Harbona. We have met him: he was one of the seven eunuchs sent to fetch Vashti at the drunken feast of chapter 1 (1:10). The servant who was there when the throne was emptied is there when the enemy falls. And he adds the detail that settles it: the gallows was built for Mordecai, whose word saved the king. Last night's reading from the chronicles is now known to the whole court. Haman had planned to hang the man the king was honouring. And the thing could not be denied, because it was standing seventy-five feet high in his garden for all Susa to see.

And the king said, Hang him on that.

verseByVerse.quote: So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Then the wrath of the king abated.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Then the wrath of the king abated.

The Psalms had long since described it: He makes a pit, digging it out, and falls into the hole that he has made. His mischief returns upon his own head (Ps 7:15-16). Whoever digs a pit will fall into it (Prov 26:27). The tree Haman raised for the righteous man held Haman.

Now look at the other tree. At the cross the reversal ran the opposite way. The tree that should have held the guilty held the righteous One: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us — for it is written, Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree (Gal 3:13). And as with Haman's gallows, the enemy's weapon turned on the enemy. None of the rulers of this age understood this, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor 2:8). On that tree Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him (Col 2:15).

Then the wrath of the king abated. It is the phrase used when the king's anger at Vashti cooled (2:1). His wrath was satisfied by the death of the guilty man. God's wrath against his people was satisfied another way, by the death of One who was not guilty: we have now been justified by his blood, and much more shall we be saved by him from the wrath of God (Rom 5:9).

And yet the chapter ends with a problem unsolved. Haman is dead. His decree is not. It is still posted in every province, sealed with the king's ring, and the law of the Medes and Persians cannot be repealed. The enemy has been removed; his sentence still stands. The next chapter is about what can be done with a law that cannot be undone.

7.theology:
The one who digs a pit falls into it (Ps 7:15-16). The enemy is undone by his own instrument, the proud man falls before the one he despised, and Esther gives up her safety to stand with her people: I and my people.

Haman's tree held the guilty; Christ's cross held the Righteous in the place of the guilty (Gal 3:13), and the enemy's weapon became his defeat (1 Cor 2:8; Col 2:15). The king's wrath abated at the death of the guilty; God's wrath toward his people is turned away by the blood of his Son (Rom 5:9).
7.examples:
The third time of asking, and the answer came.

She answered wish and request with my life and my people.

She quoted the decree's three verbs back to the king.

The king asked who dared to do what he had signed.

The man who demanded every knee bent begged a Jewish woman for his life.

Harbona, who was sent for Vashti in chapter 1, pointed to the gallows.

Haman died; his decree did not.

8.title: The Edict of Reversal: Light and Joy
8.text: <sup>1</sup>On that day King Ahasuerus gave to Queen Esther the house of Haman, the enemy of the Jews. And Mordecai came before the king, for Esther had told what he was to her.<sup>2</sup>And the king took off his signet ring, which he had taken from Haman, and gave it to Mordecai. And Esther set Mordecai over the house of Haman.<sup>3</sup>Then Esther spoke again to the king. She fell at his feet and wept and pleaded with him to avert the evil plan of Haman the Agagite and the plot that he had devised against the Jews.<sup>4</sup>When the king held out the golden scepter to Esther, Esther rose and stood before the king.<sup>5</sup>And she said, "If it please the king, and if I have found favor in his sight, and if the thing seems right before the king, and I am pleasing in his eyes, let an order be written to revoke the letters devised by Haman the Agagite, the son of Hammedatha, which he wrote to destroy the Jews who are in all the provinces of the king.<sup>6</sup>For how can I bear to see the calamity that is coming to my people? Or how can I bear to see the destruction of my kindred?"<sup>7</sup>Then King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther and to Mordecai the Jew, "Behold, I have given Esther the house of Haman, and they have hanged him on the gallows, because he intended to lay hands on the Jews.<sup>8</sup>But you may write as you please with regard to the Jews, in the name of the king, and seal it with the king's ring, for an edict written in the name of the king and sealed with the king's ring cannot be revoked."<sup>9</sup>The king's scribes were summoned at that time, in the third month, which is the month of Sivan, on the twenty-third day. And an edict was written, according to all that Mordecai commanded concerning the Jews, to the satraps and the governors and the officials of the provinces from India to Ethiopia, 127 provinces, to each province in its own script and to each people in its own language, and also to the Jews in their script and their language.<sup>10</sup>And he wrote in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed it with the king's signet ring. Then he sent the letters by mounted couriers riding on swift horses that were used in the king's service, bred from the royal stud,<sup>11</sup>saying that the king allowed the Jews who were in every city to gather and defend their lives, to destroy, to kill, and to annihilate any armed force of any people or province that might attack them, children and women included, and to plunder their goods,<sup>12</sup>on one day throughout all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar.<sup>13</sup>A copy of what was written was to be issued as a decree in every province, being publicly displayed to all peoples, and the Jews were to be ready on that day to take vengeance on their enemies.<sup>14</sup>So the couriers, mounted on their swift horses that were used in the king's service, rode out hurriedly, urged by the king's command. And the decree was issued in Susa the citadel.<sup>15</sup>Then Mordecai went out from the presence of the king in royal robes of blue and white, with a great golden crown and a robe of fine linen and purple, and the city of Susa shouted and rejoiced.<sup>16</sup>The Jews had light and gladness and joy and honor.<sup>17</sup>And in every province and in every city, wherever the king's command and his edict reached, there was gladness and joy among the Jews, a feast and a holiday. And many from the peoples of the country declared themselves Jews, for fear of the Jews had fallen on them.
8.overview: The king gives Esther Haman's house, and Mordecai, now known to be her kinsman, receives the signet ring and charge of the house (vv. 1-2). But the decree still stands. Esther falls at the king's feet in tears, is again shown the sceptre, and asks that Haman's letters be revoked: how can I bear to see the destruction of my kindred? (vv. 3-6). The king cannot revoke a sealed edict, but lets Esther and Mordecai write another in his name (vv. 7-8). On 23 Sivan Mordecai's edict goes to every province, and to the Jews in their own script, permitting them to gather and defend themselves against any force that attacks them on 13 Adar (vv. 9-14). Mordecai goes out in royal robes and a golden crown; Susa, once thrown into confusion, rejoices; the Jews have light and gladness and joy and honor, and many of the peoples declare themselves Jews (vv. 15-17).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — An Edict Sealed with the King's Ring Cannot Be Revoked
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king gives Esther Haman's house; Mordecai, now known to be her kinsman, receives the signet ring and is set over the house (vv. 1-2). Esther falls at the king's feet weeping and pleads with him to avert Haman's plot; the sceptre is held out again (vv. 3-4). For how can I bear to see the calamity that is coming to my people? (vv. 5-6). The king tells Esther and Mordecai to write as they please in his name, for an edict written in the name of the king and sealed with the king's ring cannot be revoked (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Haman was dead and his law was alive. A decree that cannot be undone can only be answered by another, with the same authority behind it.

verseByVerse.quote: On that day King Ahasuerus gave to Queen Esther the house of Haman, the enemy of the Jews. And Mordecai came before the king, for Esther had told what he was to her. And the king took off his signet ring, which he had taken from Haman, and gave it to Mordecai. And Esther set Mordecai over the house of Haman.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On that day King Ahasuerus gave to Queen Esther the house of Haman, the enemy of the Jews. And Mordecai came before the king, for Esther had told what he was to her. The same day. The house of the man who had planned to plunder every Jewish house in the empire now belongs to a Jew. The sinner's wealth is laid up for the righteous (Prov 13:22). And the cousin at the gate is brought into the king's presence as family.

And the king took off his signet ring, which he had taken from Haman, and gave it to Mordecai. And Esther set Mordecai over the house of Haman. The ring that sealed the death of the Jews is on a Jew's hand. Joseph received a ring the same way: Pharaoh took his signet ring from his hand and put it on Joseph's hand (Gen 41:42). The man who would not bow to Haman now holds Haman's authority and Haman's house.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Esther spoke again to the king. She fell at his feet and wept and pleaded with him to avert the evil plan of Haman the Agagite and the plot that he had devised against the Jews. When the king held out the golden scepter to Esther, Esther rose and stood before the king. And she said, "If it please the king, and if I have found favor in his sight, and if the thing seems right before the king, and I am pleasing in his eyes, let an order be written to revoke the letters devised by Haman the Agagite, the son of Hammedatha, which he wrote to destroy the Jews who are in all the provinces of the king. For how can I bear to see the calamity that is coming to my people? Or how can I bear to see the destruction of my kindred?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Esther spoke again to the king. She fell at his feet and wept and pleaded with him to avert the evil plan of Haman the Agagite and the plot that he had devised against the Jews.

She could have stopped. Her enemy was dead, her life was safe, her cousin was wearing the ring. But the decree still hung over every Jewish family in the empire, and she goes back in. This time she does not come in royal robes to a feast. She falls at his feet in tears.

When the king held out the golden scepter to Esther, Esther rose and stood before the king. The sceptre again. She asks with every courtesy she has — if it please the king, and if I have found favor in his sight, and if the thing seems right before the king, and I am pleasing in his eyes — and she lays the blame carefully: the letters devised by Haman, not the king who sealed them.

For how can I bear to see the calamity that is coming to my people? Or how can I bear to see the destruction of my kindred? This is the heart of an intercessor. She is safe, and she cannot live with their danger. Paul felt the same for the same people: I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart ... for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh (Rom 9:2-3). Here is a plain test to put to ourselves: is my own safety enough for me, or do I grieve for those who are not yet safe?

verseByVerse.quote: Then King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther and to Mordecai the Jew, "Behold, I have given Esther the house of Haman, and they have hanged him on the gallows, because he intended to lay hands on the Jews. But you may write as you please with regard to the Jews, in the name of the king, and seal it with the king's ring, for an edict written in the name of the king and sealed with the king's ring cannot be revoked."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther and to Mordecai the Jew, Behold, I have given Esther the house of Haman, and they have hanged him on the gallows, because he intended to lay hands on the Jews. But you may write as you please with regard to the Jews, in the name of the king, and seal it with the king's ring, for an edict written in the name of the king and sealed with the king's ring cannot be revoked.

Here is the problem, stated by the king himself. He cannot cancel his own decree. The law of the Medes and Persians, which deposed Vashti in chapter 1, now binds the king to a massacre he no longer wants (cf. Dan 6:15). What he can do is let them write another decree, with his name and his ring on it, to stand against the first.

There is a gospel shape here, and it must be drawn carefully. Haman's decree was wicked. The law's sentence on us is not; it is just. But the principle holds: a sentence that cannot be revoked must be answered, not ignored. God did not cancel the sentence on sin, and he did not pretend it was not there. By sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh (Rom 8:3), and then issued the word that answers it: There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Rom 8:1).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–17 — Light and Gladness and Joy and Honor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the twenty-third of Sivan a new edict goes out in every script and language, and to the Jews in theirs, carried by couriers on the king's swiftest horses (vv. 9-10): the Jews may gather and defend their lives against any force that attacks them on the thirteenth of Adar (vv. 11-14). Mordecai goes out in royal robes, and the city of Susa shouted and rejoiced (v. 15). The Jews had light and gladness and joy and honor; in every province there is feasting, and many declare themselves Jews (vv. 16-17).
verseByVerse.theology: In chapter 4 the Jews had four words: mourning, fasting, weeping, lamenting. Now they have four others: light, gladness, joy, honour.

verseByVerse.quote: The king's scribes were summoned at that time, in the third month, which is the month of Sivan, on the twenty-third day. And an edict was written, according to all that Mordecai commanded concerning the Jews, to the satraps and the governors and the officials of the provinces from India to Ethiopia, 127 provinces, to each province in its own script and to each people in its own language, and also to the Jews in their script and their language. And he wrote in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed it with the king's signet ring. Then he sent the letters by mounted couriers riding on swift horses that were used in the king's service, bred from the royal stud,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king's scribes were summoned at that time, in the third month, which is the month of Sivan, on the twenty-third day. The first decree was written on the thirteenth of Nisan (3:12). Count it: seventeen days to the end of Nisan, twenty-nine of Iyyar, twenty-three of Sivan — two months and ten days. Nearly nine months remain before the thirteenth of Adar.

And an edict was written, according to all that Mordecai commanded concerning the Jews, to the satraps and the governors and the officials of the provinces from India to Ethiopia, 127 provinces, to each province in its own script and to each people in its own language, and also to the Jews in their script and their language. The same scribes, the same provinces, the same imperial post — and one addition. The first decree was sent to everyone about the Jews. This one is sent to the Jews as well, in their own letters, so that every Jewish family can read with their own eyes that they may live.

Then he sent the letters by mounted couriers riding on swift horses that were used in the king's service, bred from the royal stud. The best horses in the empire. The news of life travels faster than the news of death did.

verseByVerse.quote: saying that the king allowed the Jews who were in every city to gather and defend their lives, to destroy, to kill, and to annihilate any armed force of any people or province that might attack them, children and women included, and to plunder their goods, on one day throughout all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Saying that the king allowed the Jews who were in every city to gather and defend their lives, to destroy, to kill, and to annihilate any armed force of any people or province that might attack them, children and women included, and to plunder their goods, on one day throughout all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar.

Put this beside 3:13 and you will see that Mordecai has taken Haman's decree and turned it round, verb for verb: to destroy, to kill, and to annihilate. The first decree licensed anyone to kill Jews. This one licenses Jews to defend themselves against anyone who tries.

The phrase children and women included is hard, and readers should know it is disputed. It may mirror Haman's decree and mean the families of the attackers. Or it may belong with the word them, meaning the Jews' own children and women whom the armed force would attack. Either way, the decree is for defence: it is aimed at any armed force ... that might attack them. And when the day comes, chapter 9 records that the Jews killed men who attacked them, and three times says they laid no hand on the plunder they had been permitted (9:10, 15, 16).

verseByVerse.quote: A copy of what was written was to be issued as a decree in every province, being publicly displayed to all peoples, and the Jews were to be ready on that day to take vengeance on their enemies. So the couriers, mounted on their swift horses that were used in the king's service, rode out hurriedly, urged by the king's command. And the decree was issued in Susa the citadel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A copy of what was written was to be issued as a decree in every province, being publicly displayed to all peoples, and the Jews were to be ready on that day to take vengeance on their enemies. Beside the old notice in every town square, a new one. Anyone who read the first and sharpened a knife would now read the second.

So the couriers, mounted on their swift horses that were used in the king's service, rode out hurriedly, urged by the king's command. And the decree was issued in Susa the citadel. The same hurry as before (3:15), in the opposite direction.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Mordecai went out from the presence of the king in royal robes of blue and white, with a great golden crown and a robe of fine linen and purple, and the city of Susa shouted and rejoiced.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Mordecai went out from the presence of the king in royal robes of blue and white, with a great golden crown and a robe of fine linen and purple, and the city of Susa shouted and rejoiced.

Blue and white, fine linen and purple: the colours of the king's own palace hangings in chapter 1 (1:6). The man who sat at the gate in sackcloth and ashes (4:1) walks out dressed like the palace itself. Last time he wore royal robes it was for a morning, with Haman leading his horse (6:11). These are his own.

And listen to the city. When Haman's decree went out, the city of Susa was thrown into confusion (3:15). Now the city of Susa shouted and rejoiced. When it goes well with the righteous, the city rejoices (Prov 11:10).

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews had light and gladness and joy and honor. And in every province and in every city, wherever the king's command and his edict reached, there was gladness and joy among the Jews, a feast and a holiday. And many from the peoples of the country declared themselves Jews, for fear of the Jews had fallen on them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jews had light and gladness and joy and honor.

Count the words. When the first decree arrived, the Jews in every province had four: mourning ... fasting and weeping and lamenting (4:3). Now they have four others: light and gladness and joy and honor. Every word of grief has been answered by a word of joy. Light is sown for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart (Ps 97:11). Anyone who has lived under a sentence — a diagnosis, a debt, a guilt that would not go away — and then heard it answered, knows what the Jews of Susa felt that day.

And in every province and in every city, wherever the king's command and his edict reached, there was gladness and joy among the Jews, a feast and a holiday. The same phrase as 4:3, wherever the king's command and his decree reached. The couriers had carried mourning along those roads. Now they carried feasts.

And many from the peoples of the country declared themselves Jews, for fear of the Jews had fallen on them. The book is honest about the motive: fear. Some no doubt only wanted to be on the winning side. But the prophets had seen a day coming when the nations would join themselves to this people: ten men from the nations of every tongue shall take hold of the robe of a Jew, saying, Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you (Zech 8:23). The Christian reader sees where that ends: a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb (Rev 7:9).

8.theology:
A decree that cannot be revoked must be answered by a decree of equal authority. Haman's decree was unjust and the law's sentence on sinners is just, but God has done with that sentence what the Persian king could not: carried it out on his own Son and issued the answering word, no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Rom 8:1-3).

Esther will not rest in her own safety while her kindred are in danger (Rom 9:2-3). Mourning is turned to light and joy, and the nations begin to attach themselves to God's people, as the prophets foresaw (Zech 8:23; Rev 7:9).
8.examples:
Haman's house belonged to a Jew by evening.

The ring that sealed the death of the Jews was on Mordecai's hand.

Safe herself, Esther went back in, in tears, for her people.

Even the king could not revoke his own decree.

The new edict was sent to the Jews in their own script.

Mordecai wore the palace colours of chapter 1.

Four words of grief answered by four of joy.

9.title: The Great Reversal: Victory and the Feast of Purim
9.text: <sup>1</sup>Now in the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar, on the thirteenth day of the same, when the king's command and edict were about to be carried out, on the very day when the enemies of the Jews hoped to gain the mastery over them, the reverse occurred: the Jews gained mastery over those who hated them.<sup>2</sup>The Jews gathered in their cities throughout all the provinces of King Ahasuerus to lay hands on those who sought their harm. And no one could stand against them, for the fear of them had fallen on all peoples.<sup>3</sup>All the officials of the provinces and the satraps and the governors and the royal agents also helped the Jews, for the fear of Mordecai had fallen on them.<sup>4</sup>For Mordecai was great in the king's house, and his fame spread throughout all the provinces, for the man Mordecai grew more and more powerful.<sup>5</sup>The Jews struck all their enemies with the sword, killing and destroying them, and did as they pleased to those who hated them.<sup>6</sup>In Susa the citadel itself the Jews killed and destroyed 500 men,<sup>7</sup>and also killed Parshandatha and Dalphon and Aspatha<sup>8</sup>and Poratha and Adalia and Aridatha<sup>9</sup>and Parmashta and Arisai and Aridai and Vaizatha,<sup>10</sup>the ten sons of Haman the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews, but they laid no hand on the plunder.<sup>11</sup>That very day the number of those killed in Susa the citadel was reported to the king.<sup>12</sup>And the king said to Queen Esther, "In Susa the citadel the Jews have killed and destroyed 500 men and also the ten sons of Haman. What then have they done in the rest of the king's provinces! Now what is your wish? It shall be granted you. And what further is your request? It shall be fulfilled."<sup>13</sup>And Esther said, "If it please the king, let the Jews who are in Susa be allowed tomorrow also to do according to this day's edict. And let the ten sons of Haman be hanged on the gallows."<sup>14</sup>So the king commanded this to be done. A decree was issued in Susa, and the ten sons of Haman were hanged.<sup>15</sup>The Jews who were in Susa gathered also on the fourteenth day of the month of Adar and they killed 300 men in Susa, but they laid no hands on the plunder.<sup>16</sup>Now the rest of the Jews who were in the king's provinces also gathered to defend their lives, and got relief from their enemies and killed 75,000 of those who hated them, but they laid no hands on the plunder.<sup>17</sup>This was on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar, and on the fourteenth day they rested and made that a day of feasting and gladness.<sup>18</sup>But the Jews who were in Susa gathered on the thirteenth day and on the fourteenth, and rested on the fifteenth day, making that a day of feasting and gladness.<sup>19</sup>Therefore the Jews of the villages, who live in the rural towns, hold the fourteenth day of the month of Adar as a day for gladness and feasting, as a holiday, and as a day on which they send gifts of food to one another.<sup>20</sup>And Mordecai recorded these things and sent letters to all the Jews who were in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, both near and far,<sup>21</sup>obliging them to keep the fourteenth day of the month Adar and also the fifteenth day of the same, year by year,<sup>22</sup>as the days on which the Jews got relief from their enemies, and as the month that had been turned for them from sorrow into gladness and from mourning into a holiday; that they should make them days of feasting and gladness, days for sending gifts of food to one another and gifts to the poor.<sup>23</sup>So the Jews accepted what they had started to do, and what Mordecai had written to them.<sup>24</sup>For Haman the Agagite, the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of all the Jews, had plotted against the Jews to destroy them, and had cast Pur (that is, cast lots), to crush and to destroy them.<sup>25</sup>But when it came before the king, he gave orders in writing that his evil plan that he had devised against the Jews should return on his own head, and that he and his sons should be hanged on the gallows.<sup>26</sup>Therefore they called these days Purim, after the term Pur.
