9.overview: On 13 Adar, the day Haman's lot had chosen, the reverse occurred: the Jews gather in every province to defend themselves, no one can stand against them, and the officials help them for fear of Mordecai (vv. 1-4). In Susa they kill 500 men and the ten sons of Haman, but take no plunder (vv. 5-10). At the king's fourth offer Esther asks for a second day in Susa and the public hanging of Haman's sons; 300 more are killed in Susa and 75,000 of their enemies in the provinces, and three times the text says they laid no hand on the plunder (vv. 11-16). They rest and feast on the fourteenth, in Susa on the fifteenth (vv. 17-19). Mordecai writes to make both days an annual feast of the month turned for them from sorrow into gladness, with gifts of food and gifts to the poor; it is named Purim after Haman's Pur, and the Jews bind themselves and all who join them to remember it for ever. Esther confirms it in writing (vv. 20-32).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the thirteenth of Adar, on the very day when the enemies of the Jews hoped to gain the mastery over them, the reverse occurred (v. 1). The Jews gather in every city and no one can stand against them; the officials help them for fear of Mordecai, now great in the king's house (vv. 2-4). They strike those who hated them; in Susa the citadel they kill 500 men and the ten sons of Haman, but they laid no hand on the plunder (vv. 5-10).
verseByVerse.theology: The day chosen by lot for the Jews' destruction became the day of their deliverance. The book's whole argument is in one Hebrew word: it was overturned.

verseByVerse.quote: Now in the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar, on the thirteenth day of the same, when the king's command and edict were about to be carried out, on the very day when the enemies of the Jews hoped to gain the mastery over them, the reverse occurred: the Jews gained mastery over those who hated them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now in the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar, on the thirteenth day of the same, when the king's command and edict were about to be carried out, on the very day when the enemies of the Jews hoped to gain the mastery over them, the reverse occurred: the Jews gained mastery over those who hated them.

Eleven months since the lot was cast. This is the day Haman's dice chose. And the book gives its whole theology in two Hebrew words: the reverse occurred — literally, it was overturned. The narrator does not say who overturned it. He does not need to. The day appointed for death became the day of deliverance, and every reader who has come this far knows whose hand turned it.

That is still how God works for his people. The cross was the day the enemies of God thought they had won. None of the rulers of this age understood this (1 Cor 2:8). On that day too, the reverse occurred.

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews gathered in their cities throughout all the provinces of King Ahasuerus to lay hands on those who sought their harm. And no one could stand against them, for the fear of them had fallen on all peoples. All the officials of the provinces and the satraps and the governors and the royal agents also helped the Jews, for the fear of Mordecai had fallen on them. For Mordecai was great in the king's house, and his fame spread throughout all the provinces, for the man Mordecai grew more and more powerful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jews gathered in their cities throughout all the provinces of King Ahasuerus to lay hands on those who sought their harm. And no one could stand against them, for the fear of them had fallen on all peoples. They gathered: the second decree had given them the right to band together and defend themselves, and they did. The fear of them had fallen is what Rahab said to the spies at Jericho: the fear of you has fallen upon us (Josh 2:9). Something about this people, when God was with them, made their enemies lose heart.

All the officials of the provinces and the satraps and the governors and the royal agents also helped the Jews, for the fear of Mordecai had fallen on them. For Mordecai was great in the king's house, and his fame spread throughout all the provinces. The same officials who had posted Haman's decree now protected its intended victims. The man who a year before had sat at the gate in sackcloth was the most feared man in the empire's administration.

For the man Mordecai grew more and more powerful. Those are, in Hebrew, the words used of David's rise: And David became greater and greater, for the LORD, the God of hosts, was with him (2 Sam 5:10). The narrator of Esther borrows the sentence and stops before its last clause. He will not write for the LORD was with him. He expects the reader who knows the sentence to finish it.

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews struck all their enemies with the sword, killing and destroying them, and did as they pleased to those who hated them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jews struck all their enemies with the sword, killing and destroying them, and did as they pleased to those who hated them.

This is the hard verse of the book, and it should not be hurried past. Notice first who is struck: their enemies, those who hated them, those who sought their harm (v. 2). Haman's decree was still law. In every province there were men who had spent eleven months waiting for the day they could kill Jewish families and take their houses, and on that day they came. The Jews met them. Did as they pleased is the book's recurring phrase (1:8), and here it means that for once the power was not in the hands of those who hated them.

verseByVerse.quote: In Susa the citadel itself the Jews killed and destroyed 500 men, and also killed Parshandatha and Dalphon and Aspatha and Poratha and Adalia and Aridatha and Parmashta and Arisai and Aridai and Vaizatha, the ten sons of Haman the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews, but they laid no hand on the plunder.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Susa the citadel itself the Jews killed and destroyed 500 men, and also killed Parshandatha and Dalphon and Aspatha ... the ten sons of Haman the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews. In the Hebrew scrolls these ten names are written in a column by themselves, one under another. Haman had boasted to his friends of the number of his sons (5:11). Here they are, counted.

But they laid no hand on the plunder.

The second decree had allowed it: to plunder their goods (8:11). They did not touch it. And the book says so three times (vv. 10, 15, 16). Why the insistence? Go back to Saul. Sent against Amalek, he spared Agag and the best of the sheep and of the oxen (1 Sam 15:9), and Samuel asked him, Why did you pounce on the spoil and do what was evil in the sight of the LORD? (1 Sam 15:19). Saul lost his kingdom over the plunder of Amalek. Now the family of Kish faces the house of Agag again, and this time no one takes a thing. It shows the world, and the reader, that this was not greed or robbery dressed up as self-defence. They fought for their lives and went home with nothing else.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–19 — They Laid No Hands on the Plunder
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king reports the dead in Susa and asks Esther a fourth time for her wish (vv. 11-12). She asks for one more day in Susa and for the bodies of Haman's sons to be hanged, and it is done (vv. 13-14). The Jews of Susa kill 300 more; in the provinces they gathered to defend their lives, and got relief from their enemies and killed 75,000 of those who hated them, but they laid no hands on the plunder (vv. 15-16). They rest on the fourteenth, in Susa on the fifteenth, and make it a day of feasting and gladness and sending gifts of food (vv. 17-19).
verseByVerse.theology: Three times: no hand on the plunder. Saul, sent against Amalek, was asked, Why did you pounce on the spoil? (1 Sam 15:19). The sons of Kish, facing the house of Agag, refused exactly what Saul had taken.

verseByVerse.quote: That very day the number of those killed in Susa the citadel was reported to the king. And the king said to Queen Esther, "In Susa the citadel the Jews have killed and destroyed 500 men and also the ten sons of Haman. What then have they done in the rest of the king's provinces! Now what is your wish? It shall be granted you. And what further is your request? It shall be fulfilled."
verseByVerse.commentary:
That very day the number of those killed in Susa the citadel was reported to the king. And the king said to Queen Esther, In Susa the citadel the Jews have killed and destroyed 500 men and also the ten sons of Haman. What then have they done in the rest of the king's provinces! Now what is your wish? It shall be granted you. And what further is your request? It shall be fulfilled.

The fourth time the king asks her (5:3; 5:6; 7:2). Each time he asked before, something turned. The king who once gave away a people without asking their name is now reckoning up the dead of his own capital and asking the Jewish queen what more she wants.

verseByVerse.quote: And Esther said, "If it please the king, let the Jews who are in Susa be allowed tomorrow also to do according to this day's edict. And let the ten sons of Haman be hanged on the gallows." So the king commanded this to be done. A decree was issued in Susa, and the ten sons of Haman were hanged.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Esther said, If it please the king, let the Jews who are in Susa be allowed tomorrow also to do according to this day's edict. And let the ten sons of Haman be hanged on the gallows. So the king commanded this to be done.

This request troubles many readers, and honestly so. We are not told why Esther asked. What the text shows is that there were still enemies in Susa: on the next day three hundred more men attacked and were killed (v. 15). And the sons were already dead (v. 10); hanging their bodies was the ancient way of making a public end of a house, so that no one in Susa could doubt that Haman's line was finished. The narrator does not praise the request or condemn it. Esther is not presented as sinless anywhere in this book, and we are not asked to make her so.

Nor is this a pattern for the church. Christ's people are not given a sword to wield on his behalf: the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh (2 Cor 10:4), and never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God (Rom 12:19). What the chapter describes is a persecuted minority, under a king's decree, defending itself on the day its enemies had been told they could kill it.

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews who were in Susa gathered also on the fourteenth day of the month of Adar and they killed 300 men in Susa, but they laid no hands on the plunder. Now the rest of the Jews who were in the king's provinces also gathered to defend their lives, and got relief from their enemies and killed 75,000 of those who hated them, but they laid no hands on the plunder.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jews who were in Susa gathered also on the fourteenth day of the month of Adar and they killed 300 men in Susa, but they laid no hands on the plunder. The second time.

Now the rest of the Jews who were in the king's provinces also gathered to defend their lives, and got relief from their enemies and killed 75,000 of those who hated them, but they laid no hands on the plunder. The third time. Seventy-five thousand across 127 provinces: a terrible number, and the text does not make it pleasant. But look at how it is framed: to defend their lives, those who hated them, no hands on the plunder.

And got relief is the Hebrew word for rest. Moses had joined the same three things long before: when the LORD your God has given you rest from all your enemies around you ... you shall blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven; you shall not forget (Deut 25:19). Rest from enemies, the end of Amalek, and something never to be forgotten. All three are in this chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: This was on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar, and on the fourteenth day they rested and made that a day of feasting and gladness. But the Jews who were in Susa gathered on the thirteenth day and on the fourteenth, and rested on the fifteenth day, making that a day of feasting and gladness. Therefore the Jews of the villages, who live in the rural towns, hold the fourteenth day of the month of Adar as a day for gladness and feasting, as a holiday, and as a day on which they send gifts of food to one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This was on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar, and on the fourteenth day they rested and made that a day of feasting and gladness. The Jews of Susa, who fought two days, rested on the fifteenth. That is why Purim has two dates, and why the later Jewish custom kept a second day in walled cities.

Notice which day became the feast. Not the day of the fighting. The day after, the day they rested. Purim does not celebrate killing. It celebrates rest: the morning a people woke up and found they were still alive.

Therefore the Jews of the villages, who live in the rural towns, hold the fourteenth day of the month of Adar as a day for gladness and feasting, as a holiday, and as a day on which they send gifts of food to one another. Sending portions to one another is the custom Nehemiah commanded at the reading of the law (Neh 8:10, 12). Joy that is shared.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–32 — These Days Should Be Remembered
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Mordecai writes to every Jew, near and far, to keep the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar each year, as the month that had been turned for them from sorrow into gladness and from mourning into a holiday, with feasting, gifts of food and gifts to the poor (vv. 20-23). Because Haman had cast Pur to destroy them and his plan returned on his own head, the days are called Purim (vv. 24-26); the Jews bind themselves and all who join them to keep them, that these days should be remembered and kept throughout every generation (vv. 27-28). Esther confirms it in writing, in words of peace and truth, and it is recorded (vv. 29-32).
verseByVerse.theology: Moses had said that when God gave his people rest from their enemies they must blot out the memory of Amalek and not forget (Deut 25:19). The rest came, Amalek's memory ended, and the Jews' memory of deliverance was written down to last for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: And Mordecai recorded these things and sent letters to all the Jews who were in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, both near and far, obliging them to keep the fourteenth day of the month Adar and also the fifteenth day of the same, year by year, as the days on which the Jews got relief from their enemies, and as the month that had been turned for them from sorrow into gladness and from mourning into a holiday; that they should make them days of feasting and gladness, days for sending gifts of food to one another and gifts to the poor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Mordecai recorded these things and sent letters to all the Jews who were in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, both near and far, obliging them to keep the fourteenth day of the month Adar and also the fifteenth day of the same, year by year. Letters again, down the same roads: the third set of royal letters in the book, after Haman's and the counter-decree, and this one is about a feast.

As the days on which the Jews got relief from their enemies, and as the month that had been turned for them from sorrow into gladness and from mourning into a holiday. Turned is the word of verse 1, the reverse occurred. The psalm says it of one man: You have turned for me my mourning into dancing; you have loosed my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness (Ps 30:11). Mordecai had worn the sackcloth (4:1) and then the royal robes (8:15). And Jesus promised it to his disciples on the night before the cross: You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will turn into joy (John 16:20).

That they should make them days of feasting and gladness, days for sending gifts of food to one another and gifts to the poor. The deliverance was to be remembered with generosity. Nobody was to be left out of the feast because they could not afford it.

verseByVerse.quote: So the Jews accepted what they had started to do, and what Mordecai had written to them. For Haman the Agagite, the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of all the Jews, had plotted against the Jews to destroy them, and had cast Pur (that is, cast lots), to crush and to destroy them. But when it came before the king, he gave orders in writing that his evil plan that he had devised against the Jews should return on his own head, and that he and his sons should be hanged on the gallows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the Jews accepted what they had started to do, and what Mordecai had written to them. They had already begun to feast; Mordecai made it law.

For Haman the Agagite, the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of all the Jews, had plotted against the Jews to destroy them, and had cast Pur (that is, cast lots), to crush and to destroy them. But when it came before the king, he gave orders in writing that his evil plan that he had devised against the Jews should return on his own head, and that he and his sons should be hanged on the gallows. The whole book in two sentences. And again the psalm: His mischief returns upon his own head, and on his own skull his violence descends (Ps 7:16).

When it came before the king can equally be read, in Hebrew, when she came before the king. Either way, the turning point is the same: the queen who went in uncalled, if I perish, I perish (4:16), and the plot that died when it was brought into the king's presence.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore they called these days Purim, after the term Pur. Therefore, because of all that was written in this letter, and of what they had faced in this matter, and of what had happened to them, the Jews firmly obligated themselves and their offspring and all who joined them, that without fail they would keep these two days according to what was written and at the time appointed every year, that these days should be remembered and kept throughout every generation, in every clan, province, and city, and that these days of Purim should never fall into disuse among the Jews, nor should the commemoration of these days cease among their descendants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore they called these days Purim, after the term Pur. Haman's lots. The very device he used to choose the day of their death gave its name to the feast of their deliverance. His dice are remembered every year, and only as the joke that God made of them.

The Jews firmly obligated themselves and their offspring and all who joined them, that without fail they would keep these two days. And all who joined them: the people who had declared themselves Jews (8:17) are included in the feast.

That these days should be remembered and kept throughout every generation, in every clan, province, and city, and that these days of Purim should never fall into disuse among the Jews, nor should the commemoration of these days cease among their descendants. Remembered, kept, never to fall into disuse, the memory never to cease. God had once told Moses to write this as a memorial in a book that he would blot out the memory of Amalek (Exod 17:14). Here Amalek's memory ends and Israel's memory begins.

The church has a feast of remembrance too, instituted on the night before the greatest reversal of all: Do this in remembrance of me (Luke 22:19). As often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes (1 Cor 11:26). God's people keep remembering, so that they do not forget who turned their sorrow into joy.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Queen Esther, the daughter of Abihail, and Mordecai the Jew gave full written authority, confirming this second letter about Purim. Letters were sent to all the Jews, to the 127 provinces of the kingdom of Ahasuerus, in words of peace and truth, that these days of Purim should be observed at their appointed seasons, as Mordecai the Jew and Queen Esther obligated them, and as they had obligated themselves and their offspring, with regard to their fasts and their lamenting. The command of Esther confirmed these practices of Purim, and it was recorded in writing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Queen Esther, the daughter of Abihail, and Mordecai the Jew gave full written authority, confirming this second letter about Purim. Her father's name for the second time in the book (2:15). The orphan girl who hid her people now writes to all of them, in her own name, with the authority of a queen.

Letters were sent to all the Jews, to the 127 provinces of the kingdom of Ahasuerus, in words of peace and truth, that these days of Purim should be observed at their appointed seasons ... with regard to their fasts and their lamenting. Peace and truth, fasts and lamenting turned into feasts: all of it is in Zechariah's promise that the fast of the fourth month and the fast of the fifth ... shall be to the house of Judah seasons of joy and gladness and cheerful feasts. Therefore love truth and peace (Zech 8:19). And the fasts are not forgotten. The feast remembers the sackcloth that came before it.

The command of Esther confirmed these practices of Purim, and it was recorded in writing. Written in a book, like Mordecai's deed (2:23) that was read on the sleepless night (6:1). This book has been about what gets written down and who remembers it. God's name was never written in it. His faithfulness is on every page.

9.theology:
The day chosen for destruction is overturned into the day of deliverance, and the enemy's own lot names the feast. The Jews defend their lives and refuse the plunder Saul once took from Amalek (1 Sam 15:19); the feast is kept on the day of rest, not of battle, and remembers the fasting that came before it.

Sorrow turned into joy (Ps 30:11; John 16:20) is the shape of the gospel, and the church keeps its own feast of remembrance, proclaiming the Lord's death until he comes (Luke 22:19; 1 Cor 11:26). The church does not take up the sword for Christ (2 Cor 10:4; Rom 12:19).
9.examples:
The day Haman chose became the day that was overturned.

The officials who posted Haman's decree protected the Jews.

Three times: they laid no hand on the plunder.

The feast is on the day they rested, not the day they fought.

Gifts of food to one another, and gifts to the poor.

Haman's lots named the feast.

The orphan who hid her people wrote to all of them with a queen's authority.

10.title: Mordecai's Greatness and the Hidden Hand Revealed
10.text: <sup>1</sup>King Ahasuerus imposed tax on the land and on the coastlands of the sea.<sup>2</sup>And all the acts of his power and might, and the full account of the high honor of Mordecai, to which the king advanced him, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia?<sup>3</sup>For Mordecai the Jew was second in rank to King Ahasuerus, and he was great among the Jews and popular with the multitude of his brothers, for he sought the welfare of his people and spoke peace to all his people.
10.overview: The book closes briefly. King Ahasuerus taxes his empire (v. 1); his deeds and the high honour of Mordecai are recorded in the royal chronicles of Media and Persia (v. 2); and Mordecai the Jew, second only to the king, is great among the Jews and loved by his people, for he sought the welfare of his people and spoke peace to all his people (v. 3).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — He Sought the Welfare of His People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king taxes the land and the coastlands (v. 1). His acts, and the full account of the high honor of Mordecai, are written in the chronicles of Media and Persia (v. 2). For Mordecai the Jew was second in rank to King Ahasuerus, and he was great among the Jews and popular with the multitude of his brothers, for he sought the welfare of his people and spoke peace to all his people (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The book that opened on a king displaying his glory closes on a Jew using his power for the good of others. God is not named in the last sentence either. Peace is.

verseByVerse.quote: King Ahasuerus imposed tax on the land and on the coastlands of the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
King Ahasuerus imposed tax on the land and on the coastlands of the sea.

An odd way to end, and a true one. The empire goes on; the taxes are collected; the Jews are still subjects of a Persian king. The deliverance was real, and it was not the kingdom of God. God's people are still living in someone else's empire, as they are in every age until the King comes.

verseByVerse.quote: And all the acts of his power and might, and the full account of the high honor of Mordecai, to which the king advanced him, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia?
verseByVerse.commentary:
And all the acts of his power and might, and the full account of the high honor of Mordecai, to which the king advanced him, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia?

That is the way the books of Kings close each reign: are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? (1 Kgs 14:29). Esther ends like a king's story, and the name in it beside the emperor's is a Jew's. It is the same book of chronicles where Mordecai's unrewarded deed was filed (2:23) and read aloud on the sleepless night (6:1). The man who got a line in the annals and nothing else now has a full account.

verseByVerse.quote: For Mordecai the Jew was second in rank to King Ahasuerus, and he was great among the Jews and popular with the multitude of his brothers, for he sought the welfare of his people and spoke peace to all his people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For Mordecai the Jew was second in rank to King Ahasuerus, and he was great among the Jews and popular with the multitude of his brothers, for he sought the welfare of his people and spoke peace to all his people.

Second in the empire, as Joseph had been in Egypt: only as regards the throne will I be greater than you (Gen 41:40). And the last words are not about his rank but about what he did with it. Haman used power to destroy a people; Mordecai used it to seek their good.

Sought the welfare and peace are the words of Jeremiah's letter to the first exiles: seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf (Jer 29:7). Mordecai, an exile's descendant, sought the welfare of his people. And the book, true to itself to the last line, gives us Jeremiah's words without the prayer and without the Name. The reader who has come this far can supply both.

A greater King than Ahasuerus has one at his right hand who is not second to him but one with him (Heb 1:3), and of whom Zechariah said, he shall speak peace to the nations (Zech 9:10). He came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near (Eph 2:17). Mordecai spoke peace to his own people. Christ speaks it to everyone who comes to him, and his reign has no end.

10.theology: The deliverance was real, and the empire went on; God's people still live under earthly powers. True greatness is power used for the good of others. Mordecai, second to the king, spoke peace to his people; the King whom Zechariah promised speaks peace to the nations (Zech 9:10; Eph 2:17).
10.examples:
The last chapter opens with taxes.

Mordecai's story closes with the formula of the kings of Judah.

Jeremiah's words to the exiles, without the prayer and without the Name.

The last word of the book is peace.
